Among its lessons: tolerating the poor manners, ignorance, and harshness of the envoy of the disbelievers, and not retaliating against it, because of the general interest involved. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not retaliate against 'Urwah for taking hold of his beard during his speech, even though that was the custom of the Arabs. But dignity and glorification are contrary to that.

Likewise, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not retaliate against the two envoys of Musaylimah when they said: "We testify that he is the Messenger of Allah," and he said: "Were it not that envoys are not killed, I would have killed you both."

Among its lessons: the purity of phlegm, whether it comes from the head or the chest.

Among its lessons: the purity of water that has been used (for ritual purification).

Among its lessons: it is recommended to seek omens of good (*tafa'ul*), and that it is not of the disliked superstition (*tiyarah*), because of his saying when Suhayl came: "Your affair has become easy (*sahula amrukum*)."

Among its lessons: when the one testified against is known by his name and his father's name, that suffices without mentioning the grandfather, because the Prophet (ﷺ) did not add to "Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah," and he was content from Suhayl with mentioning his name and his father's name only. Requiring mention of the grandfather has no basis. When al-'Adda' ibn Khalid bought the slave from him (ﷺ), he wrote for him: "This is what al-'Adda' ibn Khalid ibn Hawdhah bought," and he mentioned his grandfather. This is an addition of clarification, which indicates that it is permissible and there is no harm in it, but it does not indicate that it is a requirement. And since he was not so famous that his name and his father's name would suffice, he mentioned his grandfather. Therefore, mention of the grandfather is required when the name and the father's name are shared with another, and when they are not shared, the name and father's name suffice. And Allah knows best.

Among its lessons: the reconciliation with the polytheists by means of some terms that involve injustice to the Muslims is permissible, for a preponderant benefit and to repel what is worse than it. In this there is the averting of the greater of two evils by bearing the lesser of them.

Among its lessons: whoever swears to do something, or vows it, or promises it to another, without specifying a time, neither explicitly nor in his intention, it is not required to be done immediately, but rather at one's leisure (*'ala al-taraakhi*).

Among its lessons: shaving the head is an act of worship (*nusuk*), and it is better than cutting it short (*taqsir*), and it is an act of worship in the 'umrah just as it is in the hajj, and it is an act of worship in the 'umrah of the one prevented (*muhsar*) just as it is in the 'umrah of others.

Among its lessons: the one prevented slaughters his offering wherever he is prevented, whether in the lawful area or the sacred area. He is not obligated to arrange with someone to slaughter it in the sacred area if he cannot reach it. He does not leave the state of ihram until he reaches its place of sacrifice (*mahall*), on the evidence of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the offering held back from reaching its place of sacrifice﴾ [al-Fath: 25].

Among its lessons: the place where he (ﷺ) slaughtered the offering was from the lawful area, not from the sacred area, because the whole sacred area is a place of sacrifice (*mahall al-hady*).

Among its lessons: the one prevented is not obligated to make up the pilgrimage (*qada'*), because he (ﷺ) commanded them to shave and slaughter, and he did not command any of them to make it up. The 'umrah of the following year was neither obligatory nor a makeup for the 'umrah of the prevention, for they were in the 'umrah of the prevention about fourteen hundred, and in the 'umrah of the *qadiyyah* fewer than that. It was called the 'umrah of *al-qadiyyah* and *al-qada'* only because it was the 'umrah over which he made the agreement with them, so the 'umrah was attributed to the verbal noun of its act.

Among its lessons: a command in absolute form requires immediate compliance (*'ala al-fawr*), otherwise he would not have been angry at their delaying compliance beyond the time of the command. It has been argued regarding their delay in compliance that they were hoping for abrogation (*naskh*), so they delayed, interpreting it that way. This excuse is more fitting to be excused from, and it is false. For if he (ﷺ) had understood this from them, his anger would not have been so severe over the delay of his command, and he would have said:

"What is wrong with me that I should not be angry, when I command a command and I am not obeyed?"

Their delay was only from a striving that is forgiven, not one that is thanked. And Allah was pleased with them, forgave them, and made Paradise obligatory for them.

Among its lessons: the basic principle is that his community shares with him in the rulings, except what the evidence particularizes. For this reason Umm Salamah said: "Go out and do not speak to anyone until you shave your head and slaughter your offering," and she knew that the people would follow him.

If it is said: How did they act in imitation of his deed when they had not complied when he commanded them? It is said: This is the reason for which whoever thought that they delayed compliance hoping for abrogation thought so. But when the Prophet (ﷺ) did that, they knew then that it was a settled ruling, not abrogated. The falsity of this assumption has already been mentioned. However, when he became angry at them and went out without speaking to them, and showed them that he had hastened to comply with what he had been commanded, and that he had not delayed as they had delayed, and that their following him and obeying him requires their imitation of him, then they hastened at that point to imitate him and comply with his command.

Among its lessons: it is permissible to make a peace agreement with the disbelievers on the condition of returning whoever comes from them to the Muslims, and that whoever goes from the Muslims to them is not returned. This applies to men, not women. As for women, it is not permissible to stipulate their return to the disbelievers, and this is the specific place of abrogation (*naskh*) in this contract, by the explicit text of the Qur'an. There is no way to claim abrogation elsewhere without a valid basis.

Among its lessons: the dissolution of a woman's private part from the ownership of the husband is of value (*mutaqawwim*), and for this reason Allah, glorified be He, obligated the return of the dower to one whose wife emigrated and was kept from him, and to one whose Muslim wife apostatized, when the disbelievers were entitled to demand the return of the dowers of those wives who had emigrated to them. He informed that this is the ruling He decreed among them, and then nothing abrogated it. In His obligating the return of what the husbands had given, there is evidence that its value is by the stated amount (*al-musamma*), not by the customary dower (*mahr al-mithl*).

Among its lessons: the return of those who come from the disbelievers to the leader does not include those who leave them as Muslims for a land other than the leader's land. And if one comes to the leader's land, it is not obligatory to return him without a request. For the Prophet (ﷺ) did not return Abu Basir when he came to him, nor did he compel him to go back. But when they came seeking him, he allowed them to take him and did not compel him to return.

Among its benefits: if the treaty-bound (mu'ahadun) people took custody of him and gained control over him, and then he killed one of them, he is not liable for blood money (diyah) or retaliation (qawad), and the Imam is not liable for him either. His ruling in this case is the same as the ruling on killing them in their own lands, where the Imam has no authority over them. Abu Basir killed one of the two treaty-bound men at Dhu al-Hulayfah, which is part of Madinah's territory, but they had already taken custody of him and he was separated from the hand and authority of the Imam.

Another benefit: if the treaty-bound people make a covenant with the Imam, and a group of them breaks away, fights others and seizes their property, without joining the Imam, the Imam is not obliged to repel them from those people or to prevent them from doing so. This holds whether or not they entered the Imam's contract, covenant and religion. The treaty between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the polytheists was not a treaty between Abu Basir and his companions and them. On this basis, if there is a treaty between some of the rulers of the Muslims and some of the protected people (ahl al-dhimmah) of the Christians and others, another Muslim ruler may raid them and seize their property if he has no treaty with them. This is what Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) ruled concerning the Christians of Malatya and their captivity, citing the story of Abu Basir with the polytheists as evidence.

[Section: On pointing out some of the wisdoms contained in this truce]

These wisdoms are too great and too lofty for anyone to encompass them except Allah, who perfected their causes, so the outcome came about in the manner that His wisdom and praiseworthiness required.

Among them: it was a prelude before the Great Victory (al-fath al-a'zam), through which Allah honoured His Messenger and his army, and through which people entered the religion of Allah in multitudes. This truce was thus a gateway to it, a key to it, and a herald before it. This is Allah's custom, glorified is He, in great matters that He decrees by destiny and by law: He prepares for them, before they occur, preliminary steps and preparations that announce them and point to them.

Among them: this truce was among the greatest conquests. People became secure from one another, Muslims mixed with the disbelievers, they approached them with the call and made them hear the Qur'an, they debated with them about Islam openly and securely, those who had been concealing their Islam came forth, and whoever Allah willed to enter it entered it during the truce period. For this reason Allah called it a "manifest victory." Ibn Qutaybah said: "We have decreed for you a great decree." Mujahid said: "It is what Allah decreed for him at al-Hudaybiyyah."

The reality of the matter is that fath, linguistically, means opening what is closed. The settlement that took place with the polytheists at al-Hudaybiyyah was closed and locked until Allah opened it. Among the causes of its opening was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions were prevented from the House. In its outward appearance it was humiliation and subjugation for the Muslims, but inwardly it was might, victory and triumph. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was looking beyond it to the great victory, might and triumph, as though through a thin veil. He gave the polytheists every condition they asked of him, conditions that most of his companions and their leaders could not bear, while he (ﷺ) knew what beloved good was contained within this disliked matter: ﴿But it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216].

It was said in verse:
"Often the thing the souls dislike
Becomes the cause of what they love, the like of which is no cause."

So he entered upon those conditions with the confidence of one who trusts in Allah's support and aid for him, and that the final outcome belongs to him, and that those conditions and bearing them were in fact victory itself. This was among the greatest forces that those who imposed the conditions had raised and set up against themselves while they were unaware. They were humiliated from the very place where they sought might, and they were subdued from the very place where they displayed power, pride and dominance. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the armies of Islam were honoured from the very place where they were broken for the sake of Allah and bore humiliation for His sake and in Him. Thus the tables turned, the matter was reversed, the might of falsehood was transformed into humiliation in truth, and the breaking for the sake of Allah was transformed into might through Allah. The wisdom and signs of Allah appeared, along with the confirmation of His promise and the support of His Messenger, in the most complete and perfect forms, beyond which the intellect has no further suggestion.

Among them: what He, glorified is He, caused for the believers of increased faith, submission and compliance in what they loved and what they disliked, and the contentment they attained with the decree of Allah, the confirmation of His promise, their waiting for what they had been promised, and their witnessing Allah's favour and blessing upon them through the tranquillity (sakinah) He sent down into their hearts, at a time when they most needed it, in that situation which shakes mountains. So Allah sent down upon them from His tranquillity that by which their hearts were reassured, their souls were strengthened, and they increased in faith through it.

Among them: He, glorified is He, made this ruling, which He passed for His Messenger and the believers, a cause for what He mentioned: the forgiveness for His Messenger of his past and future sins, the completion of His blessing upon him, His guidance to the straight path, His granting him a mighty victory, His pleasure with him, his entering under it, and the expansion of his chest through it, despite the humiliation in it and his granting what they asked. These were among the causes by which the Messenger and his companions attained those things. For this reason Allah, glorified is He, mentioned them as a reward and an end, and this occurs only through an act performed by the Messenger and the believers at the time of Allah's judgment and His conquest.

Reflect on how He, glorified is He, described the victory as "mighty" in this situation, then mentioned the sending down of tranquillity into the hearts of the believers in this situation in which hearts were shaken and became most deeply anxious. They were then most in need of tranquillity, so they increased in faith upon their faith. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned their pledge to His Messenger and confirmed it by making it a pledge to Him, glorified is He, and that the hand of Allah, exalted is He, was above their hands, since the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was like that, and he was His Messenger and Prophet. So the contract with him is a contract with the One who sent him, and his pledge is His pledge. Whoever pledges allegiance to him has in effect pledged allegiance to Allah, and the hand of Allah is above his hand. If "the Black Stone is the right hand of Allah on earth, so whoever shakes hands with it and kisses it, it is as though he shook hands with Allah and kissed His right hand," then the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is more deserving of this than the Black Stone. Then He informed that the one who breaks this pledge only harms himself, and that the one who fulfils it has a great reward. Every believer has pledged allegiance to Allah through the tongue of His Messenger, a pledge to Islam and its rights, so there are those who break it and those who fulfil it.

Then He mentioned the condition of those Bedouins who stayed behind from him, and their having the worst opinion of Allah, that He would forsake His Messenger, his allies and his army, and give their enemy victory over them, so that they would never return to their families. This was due to their ignorance of Allah, His names and attributes, and what befits Him, and their ignorance of His Messenger and what his Lord and Master is worthy to treat him with.

Then He, glorified is He, informed of His pleasure with the believers for entering under the pledge to His Messenger, and that He, glorified is He, knew what was in their hearts at that time of truthfulness, loyalty, complete submission and obedience, and of preferring Allah and His Messenger over anything else. So Allah sent down tranquillity, peace and contentment into their hearts, and rewarded them for their contentment with His judgment and their patience with His command with a near victory and many spoils that they would take. The first of the victory and spoils was the conquest of Khaybar and its spoils. Then the victories and spoils continued until the end of time.

He promised them many spoils that they would take, and informed them that He had hastened this spoil for them.

There are two opinions about it. The first is that it refers to the truce that took place between them and their enemy. The second is that it refers to the conquest of Khaybar and its spoils.

Then He said: ﴿And He restrained the hands of the people from you﴾.

It was said: the hands of the people of Makkah, that they should fight them.

It was also said: the hands of the Jews, when they intended to assassinate those in Madinah after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had left it with those of the Companions who were with him. It was also said: they are the people of Khaybar and their allies who wanted to help them, from Asad and Ghatafan. The sound view is that the verse includes all of them.

As for His saying: ﴿And that it may be a sign for the believers﴾:

It was said: this act which He performed for you, namely restraining the hands of your enemies from you despite their great number, since at that time the people of Makkah and those around it, the people of Khaybar and those around it, Asad, Ghatafan, and most of the tribes of the Arabs were enemies to them, and they were among them like a mole on the skin (*al-shamah*). Yet they did not reach them with any harm. So among the signs of Allah, glorified is He, is the restraining of their enemies' hands from them, so that they did not reach them with harm despite their great number and the severity of their hostility, and His taking charge of guarding and protecting them whether they were present or absent.

It was also said: it refers to the conquest of Khaybar, which He made a sign for His believing servants and a token of what would follow it of conquests. For Allah, glorified is He, had promised them many spoils and great conquests, so He hastened for them the conquest of Khaybar, and made it a sign of what would follow it, and a reward for their patience and contentment on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah, and a thanks. For this reason He specified it, and its spoils, for those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyyah.

Then He said: ﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾.

So He combined for them, along with victory, triumph and spoils, guidance. He made them guided, victorious, and gaining spoils. Then He promised them many spoils and other conquests which they were not yet able to attain at that time. It was said: these are Makkah; it was said: they are Persia and Rome.

It was also said: the conquests that came after Khaybar are from the eastern and western parts of the earth.

[Section: On the Expedition of Khaybar]

Musa ibn ʿUqbah said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to Madinah from al-Hudaybiyyah, he stayed there about twenty nights or close to that, then he set out as a raider towards Khaybar. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had promised him it while he was at al-Hudaybiyyah.

Malik said: the conquest of Khaybar took place in the sixth year, but the majority hold that it was in the seventh.

Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm asserted that it was in the sixth year without doubt. Perhaps the disagreement is based on the starting point of the calendar: is it the month of Rabiʿ al-Awwal, the month of his arrival in Madinah, or Muharram at the beginning of the year? People have two approaches to this:

The majority hold that the calendar began with Muharram, while Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm holds that it began with Rabiʿ al-Awwal, when he arrived. (The first to date by the Hijrah was Yaʿla ibn Umayyah in Yemen), as Imam Ahmad narrated it with a sound chain.

It was also said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, in the sixteenth year of the Hijrah.

Ibn Ishaq said: al-Zuhri narrated to me from ʿUrwah, from Marwan ibn al-Hakam and al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, that both of them narrated to him, saying: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, and the Surah of Victory (al-Fath) was revealed to him between Makkah and Madinah, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave him Khaybar through it, ﴿Allah has promised you many spoils that you will take, and has hastened this for you﴾ [al-Fath: 20], which is Khaybar. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah in Dhu al-Hijjah, and stayed there until he set out for Khaybar in Muharram. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ halted at al-Raji', a valley between Khaybar and Ghatafan, and feared that Ghatafan would support them, so he spent the night there until morning, then set out towards them. End of quote.

He appointed Siba' ibn ʿUrfutah as his deputy over Madinah. Abu Hurayrah arrived in Madinah at that time and met Siba' ibn ʿUrfutah at the dawn prayer, and he heard him recite in the first rak'ah: *Kaf-Ha-Ya-ʿAyn-Sad*, and in the second: *Woe to those who give less* (al-Mutaffifin). So he said to himself: Woe to so-and-so, he has two measures: when he takes by measure he takes in full, and when he gives by measure he gives short. When he had finished his prayer, he went to Siba' and provided him, until he reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and spoke to the Muslims, and they included him and his companions in their shares.

Salamah ibn al-Akwa' said: "We set out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ towards Khaybar, and we travelled by night. A man from the people said to ʿAmir ibn al-Akwaʿ: Will you not make us hear some of your verses?

ʿAmir was a poet, so he dismounted and began to drive the camels for the people, saying:

*O Allah, had it not been for You, we would not have been guided,*
*nor would we have given charity or prayed.*
*So forgive, as a ransom for You, what we have committed,*
*and make our feet firm if we meet [the enemy].*
*And send down tranquillity upon us,*
*for when a cry is raised against us, we come.*
*They sought to overwhelm us with the cry,*
*but if they desire strife, we refuse.*

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Who is this driver?" They said: ʿAmir. He said: "May Allah have mercy on him." A man from the people said: "He has become a martyr (*wajibat*), O Messenger of Allah! Why did you not let us benefit from him?" He said: So we came to Khaybar and besieged them until severe hunger afflicted us. Then Allah, Exalted is He, granted us victory over them. When evening came, they lit many fires. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What are these fires? On what are you lighting them?"

They said: "On meat."

He said: "On what meat?"

They said: "On the meat of domestic donkeys."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Spill it and break the pots." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we spill it and wash them?" He said: "Or that?"

When the two sides lined up, Marhab came out swaggering with his sword, saying:

*Khaybar knows that I am Marhab,*
*armed, a brave and experienced warrior,*
*when the wars come blazing.*

ʿAmir came down to him saying:

*Khaybar knows that I am ʿAmir,*
*armed, a brave warrior who plunges in.*

They exchanged two blows. Marhab's sword struck the shield of ʿAmir, and ʿAmir moved to strike him from below, but his sword was short, so its edge turned back upon him and struck the knee-joint, and he died from it. Salamah said to the Prophet ﷺ: "They claim that ʿAmir's deeds have been nullified." He said: "The one who said that is a liar. He has two rewards," and he joined his two fingers together, "he is truly a striver and a fighter. Few Arabs have walked with it as he did."

[Section: On the Arrival at Khaybar]

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived at Khaybar, he prayed the dawn prayer there, and the Muslims mounted up. The people of Khaybar came out with their hoes and baskets, not realising, for they had gone out to their lands. When they saw the army, they said: "Muhammad, by Allah! Muhammad and the army!" Then they returned fleeing to their fortresses. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah is greatest, Khaybar is ruined! Allah is greatest, Khaybar is ruined! When we descend into the courtyard of a people, the morning of those who were warned is evil."

When the Prophet ﷺ drew near and overlooked it, he said: "Halt." The army halted, and he said:

"O Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and what they overshadow, and Lord of the seven earths and what they carry, and Lord of the devils and what they lead astray. We ask You for the good of this town, the good of its people, and the good of what is in it, and we seek refuge in You from the evil of this town, the evil of its people, and the evil of what is in it. Advance in the name of Allah."

On the night of the entry, he said: "I will surely give this banner tomorrow to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love; Allah will grant victory through his hands." The people spent the night discussing among themselves which of them would be given it. When morning came, the people all went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ hoping to be given it. He said: "Where is ʿAli ibn Abi Talib?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, he has an eye complaint." He said: "Send for him."

He was brought, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spat in his eyes and prayed for him, and he was healed as though he had never had any pain. He gave him the banner. ʿAli said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I fight them until they become like us?" He said: "Proceed calmly until you alight in their courtyard, then call them to Islam, and inform them of what is incumbent upon them of Allah's right in it. By Allah, for Allah to guide one man through you is better for you than red camels."

Marhab came out saying:

*I am the one whom my mother named Marhab,*
*armed, a brave and experienced warrior,*
*when the wars come blazing.*

ʿAli came out to him saying:

*I am the one whom my mother named Haydarah,*
*like a lion of thickets, of fearsome appearance,*
*I give them full measure, like the sandara measure.*

He struck Marhab and split his skull, and that was the conquest.

When ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, drew near their fortresses, a Jew looked out from the top of the fortress and said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am ʿAli ibn Abi Talib." The Jew said: "You have prevailed, but what was sent down to Musa was not..." [the Jew said this in mockery, meaning: you have overcome, but the Torah was not given to you].

This is how it is in *Sahih Muslim* that "ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, is the one who killed Marhab." Musa ibn ʿUqbah said, on the authority of al-Zuhri and Abu al-Aswad, from ʿUrwah; and Yunus ibn Bukayr, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Sahl, one of the Banu Harithah, narrated to me, on the authority of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, that Muhammad ibn Maslamah was the one who killed him." Jabir said in his narration: "Marhab the Jew came out of the fortress of Khaybar, having gathered his weapons, and he was chanting verse and saying: Who will duel? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Who will deal with this? Muhammad ibn Maslamah said: I will, O Messenger of Allah. By Allah, I am the one who seeks vengeance and avenges, they killed my brother yesterday," meaning Mahmud ibn Maslamah, who had been killed at Khaybar. He said: "Go out to him, O Allah, help him against him." When each of them drew close to the other, a tree came between them, and each of them took cover behind it from the other. Whenever one took cover behind it from the other, the other cut away what was in front of him from it with his sword, until each of them came out facing the other, and between them the tree became like a standing man with no branches on it. Then he (Marhab) charged at Muhammad and struck him, but he guarded himself with the shield, and his sword became stuck in it, and it clamped down on it and held it. Then Muhammad ibn Maslamah struck him and killed him." Likewise, Salamah ibn Salamah and Majmaʿ ibn Harithah said that Muhammad ibn Maslamah killed Marhab.

Al-Waqidi said: It was also said: "Muhammad ibn Maslamah struck the two legs of Marhab and cut them off, and Marhab said: Finish me off, O Muhammad. Muhammad said: Taste death as my brother Mahmud tasted it." He passed by him, and ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, passed by him, struck his neck and took his spoils. They disputed before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over his spoils. Muhammad ibn Maslamah said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not cut off his legs and leave him except so that he might taste death, and I was able to finish him off." ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "He has spoken the truth. I struck his neck after he had cut off his legs." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave Muhammad ibn Maslamah his sword, spear, helmet and shield.

The sword of Marhab was among the family of Muhammad ibn Maslamah, and in it was a writing that no one knew the meaning of, until a Jew read it, and in it was:

*This is the sword of Marhab;*
*whoever tastes it will perish.*

Then, after Marhab, his brother Yasir came out, and al-Zubayr came out against him. Safiyyah, his mother, said: "O Messenger of Allah, is he going to kill my son?" He said: "Rather, your son will kill him, if Allah wills." Then al-Zubayr killed him.

Musa ibn ʿUqbah said: Then the Jews entered a fortress of theirs that was impregnable, called al-Qamus. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ besieged them for about twenty nights. It was a pestilential land of severe heat, and the Muslims suffered greatly. They slaughtered the donkeys, but the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade them from eating them. A black Abyssinian slave from the people of Khaybar, who had been tending sheep for his master, came. When he saw the people of Khaybar had taken up weapons, he asked them: "What do you want?"

They said: "We will fight this man who claims to be a prophet." Thoughts of the Prophet ﷺ came into his heart. He came with his sheep to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "What do you say, and what do you call to?" He said: "I call to Islam, and that you testify that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah, and that you worship none but Allah."

The slave said: "What do I gain if I testify and believe in Allah, Mighty and Majestic?" He said: "Paradise for you, if you die upon that."

He took Islam and then said, "O Messenger of God, these sheep are a trust I hold." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him, "Take them out from your possession and throw pebbles at them, for God will discharge your trust on your behalf." He did so, and the sheep returned to their owner. The Jew then knew that his slave had embraced Islam.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood among the people, admonished them, and urged them to jihad (striving in the way of God, including armed fighting). When the Muslims and the Jews met in battle, among those killed was the black slave. The Muslims carried him to their encampment, and he was placed in the fustat (a tent). They reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) looked into the tent, then turned to his companions and said: "God has honoured this slave and led him to good. I saw by his head two of the wide-eyed houris, and he never once prostrated to God."

Hammad ibn Salamah said, on the authority of Thabit, from Anas: "A man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said, 'O Messenger of God, I am a man of black complexion, ugly of face, foul of smell, and I have no wealth. If I fight these people until I am killed, will I enter Paradise?' He said, 'Yes.'

So he advanced, fought until he was killed. The Prophet (ﷺ) came upon him while he was slain and said, 'God has beautified your face, perfumed your scent, and multiplied your wealth.' Then he said, 'I saw his two wives from the wide-eyed houris pulling off his robe, entering between his skin and his robe.'"

Shaddad ibn al-Hadi said: "A man from the Bedouin came to the Prophet (ﷺ), believed in him and followed him, and said, 'I will migrate with you.' So he (the Prophet) entrusted him to some of his companions. When the expedition of Khaybar came, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took some booty and divided it, and he set aside a share for the Bedouin. His companions gave him what had been set aside for him, and he was tending their animals. When he came, they handed it to him. He said, 'What is this?' They said, 'A share the Messenger of God (ﷺ) set aside for you.' He took it and came with it to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, 'What is this, O Messenger of God?' He said, 'A share I set aside for you.' He said, 'It was not on this basis that I followed you; rather, I followed you on condition that I be struck here,' and he pointed to his throat, 'by an arrow, so that I die and enter Paradise.' He (the Prophet) said, 'If you are truthful to God, He will be truthful to you.' Then he rose to fight the enemy, and he was brought to the Prophet (ﷺ) while slain. He said, 'Is it him?' They said, 'Yes.' He said, 'He was truthful to God, so God has been truthful to him.' The Prophet (ﷺ) shrouded him in his own robe, then put him forward and prayed over him. Among his supplications for him was: 'O God, this is Your servant who went out as a migrant in Your way; he was killed as a martyr, and I am a witness to it.'"

Al-Waqidi said: "The Jews moved to the fortress of al-Zubayr, a strong stronghold on the top of a hill. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) stayed there three days. A Jewish man called Azal came and said, 'O Abu al-Qasim, even if you remained for a month, they would not care. They have a water supply and springs beneath the earth; they come out at night, drink from them, then return to their fortress and hold out against you. If you cut off their water supply, they will come out to you.' So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) marched to their water, cut it off from them. When it was cut off, they came out and fought the fiercest fight. Some of the Muslims were killed, and about ten Jews were struck down. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) conquered it. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) moved to the people of al-Kutaybah, al-Watih and al-Salalim, the fortress of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq. Its people fortified themselves most strongly, and every fugitive who had fled from al-Natat and al-Shiqq came to them. Khaybar had two parts: the first was al-Shiqq and al-Natat, which he had conquered first; the second part was al-Kutaybah, al-Watih and al-Salalim. They would not come out from their fortresses until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) intended to set up the mangonel against them. When they became certain of destruction, after the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had besieged them for fourteen days, they asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for peace. Ibn Abi al-Huqayq sent to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'Shall I come down and speak with you?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, 'Yes.' Ibn Abi al-Huqayq came down and made peace with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on condition that the blood of those among them who were fighting men in their fortresses be spared, and that the children be left to them, and that they leave Khaybar and its land with their offspring, and that they leave the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in possession of whatever wealth and land they had, along with the gold, the silver, the weapons and the armour, except for a garment on a person's back. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'The protection of God and the protection of His Messenger is withdrawn from you if you conceal anything from me.' They made peace with him on that basis."

Hammad ibn Salamah said: Ubayd Allah ibn Umar informed us, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) fought the people of Khaybar until he drove them into their castle, and he took control of the crops, the palm trees and the land. They made peace with him on condition that they be expelled from it, and that they keep whatever their mounts could carry, while the gold and silver belonged to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He stipulated that they must not conceal or hide anything, and if they did, they would have no protection and no covenant. They then hid a leather bag containing wealth and jewelry belonging to Huyayy ibn Akhtab, which he had brought with him to Khaybar when al-Nadir were expelled. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to the paternal uncle of Huyayy ibn Akhtab: 'What became of the leather bag of Huyayy which he brought from al-Nadir?' He said: 'Expenses and wars have consumed it.' He said: 'The covenant is recent, and the wealth is more than that.' So he handed him over to al-Zubayr, who tormented him. Before this, Huyayy had entered a ruin and said: 'I have seen Huyayy circling in a ruin here.' They went and searched, and found the bag in the ruin. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) then killed the two sons of Abu al-Huqayq, one of whom was the husband of Safiyyah bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) took captive their women and children, and divided their property, because of the breach of covenant they had committed. He intended to expel them from it, but they said: 'O Muhammad, let us remain in this land, to cultivate it and tend it, for we know it better than you.'

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions had no servants to tend it, and they could not devote themselves to tending it. So he gave them Khaybar on condition that they receive half of every crop and every fruit, for as long as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wished to let them remain. Abd Allah ibn Rawahah used to estimate its produce for them, as has been mentioned earlier. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not kill anyone after the peace except the two sons of Abu al-Huqayq, because of the breach of covenant they had committed; for they had stipulated that if they concealed or hid anything, the protection of God and of His Messenger would be withdrawn from them. They hid something, so he said to them: 'Where is the wealth you took out of Madinah when we expelled you?' They said: 'It is gone.' They swore to that, but the cousin of Kinanah admitted to the wealth against the two of them, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) handed him over to al-Zubayr to torment him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) then handed Kinanah over to Muhammad ibn Maslamah, who killed him." It is said that Kinanah was the one who had killed the brother of Mahmud ibn Maslamah.

"The Messenger of God (ﷺ) took captive Safiyyah bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab and the daughter of her paternal aunt. Safiyyah had been married to Kinanah ibn Abi al-Huqayq, and she was a recent bride who had only just consummated the marriage. He ordered Bilal to take her to his camp, and Bilal passed by her amid the slain. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) disliked that and said: 'Has mercy been removed from you, O Bilal?!'"

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) offered her Islam, and she embraced it. He chose her for himself, freed her, and made her freedom her bridal gift. He consummated the marriage with her on the way and held a wedding feast for her. He noticed a greenish mark on her face and said: "What is this?" She said: "O Messenger of God, before you came to us, I saw in a dream that the moon had moved from its place and fallen into my lap. By God, I do not remember anything else about you." She recounted it to her husband, and he slapped her face and said: "You long for this king who is in Madinah!"

The Companions doubted whether he had taken her as a concubine or as a wife. They said: "Look: if he veils her, then she is one of his wives; otherwise she is among those whom his right hand owns." When he mounted, he placed his garment over her back and face, then tied its end beneath her. They then held back from him on the journey, and knew that she was one of his wives. When he came to lift her onto the mount, she out of reverence for him avoided placing her foot on his thigh, so she placed her knee on his thigh, then rode.

When he had consummated the marriage with her, Abu Ayyub spent the night standing near his tent, holding the hilt of his sword until morning. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came out and Abu Ayyub saw him, he exclaimed "Allahu akbar" upon seeing him come out. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked him: "What is wrong with you, Abu Ayyub?" He said: "O Messenger of God, I could not sleep last night when you entered upon this woman. I remembered that you had killed her father, her brother, her husband and most of her clan, so I feared that she might assassinate you." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) laughed and said something kind to him.

[The story of a Jewish woman poisoning the Prophet (ﷺ)]

During this campaign, "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was poisoned. Zaynab bint al-Harith, the Jewess, wife of Sallam ibn Mishkam, presented him with a roasted sheep that she had poisoned. She asked: 'Which meat does he love most?' They said: 'The foreleg.' So she put a great deal of poison in the foreleg. When he bit into its meat, the foreleg informed him that it was poisoned. He spat out the morsel, then said: 'Gather for me all the Jews who are here.' They were gathered for him, and he said to them: 'I am going to ask you about something; will you be truthful with me about it?' They said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'Who is your father?' They said: 'Our father is so-and-so.' He said: 'You lie; your father is so-and-so.' They said: 'You have spoken the truth and done good.' He said: 'Will you be truthful with me about something if I ask you about it?' They said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim, and if we lie to you, you will recognise our lie just as you recognised it concerning our father.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Who are the people of the Fire?' They said: 'We will remain in it for a short time, and then you will succeed us in it.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'Be silent and remain there; by God, we will never succeed you in it, ever.'

Then he said: 'Will you be truthful with me about something if I ask you about it?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Did you put poison in this sheep?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What led you to do that?' They said: 'We intended, if you were a liar, that we would be rid of you; and if you were a prophet, it would not harm you.'"

"The woman was brought to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and she said: 'I intended to kill you.' He said: 'God would not have empowered you over me.' They said: 'Shall we not kill her?' He said: 'No.' He did not hold her to account and did not punish her." He had himself cupped on the shoulder blade, and he ordered those who had eaten from it to be cupped, and some of them died. There was disagreement about whether the woman was killed. Al-Zuhri said: "She embraced Islam, so he left her alone." Abd al-Razzaq reported this from Ma'mar from him. Then Ma'mar said: "The people say the Prophet (ﷺ) killed her."

Abu Dawud said: Wahb ibn Baqiyyah narrated to us, saying: Khalid narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Amr, from Abu Salamah, that "a Jewish woman in Khaybar presented the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a roasted sheep." He mentioned the story and said: "Bishr ibn al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur died, so he sent to the Jewish woman: 'What led you to do what you did?'" Jabir said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered her to be brought, and she was killed."

I say: both reports are mursal (lacking a companion in the chain). Hammad ibn Salamah related it from Muhammad ibn Amr, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, in a connected form, that he killed her when Bishr ibn al-Bara' died.

The two reports have been reconciled by saying that he did not kill her at first, but when Bishr died, he killed her.

There is disagreement as to whether the Prophet (ﷺ) ate from it or did not eat. Most reports say that he ate from it, and he remained after that for three years, until in the illness in which he died he said: "I have continued to feel the effect of the morsel I ate from the sheep on the day of Khaybar; this is the time of the severing of my aorta."

Al-Zuhri said: "So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) died as a martyr."

Musa ibn 'Uqba and others said: When the Quraysh heard that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had set out for Khaybar, there was a great dispute and wagering among them. Some said, "Muhammad and his companions will prevail." Others said, "The two allies and the Jews of Khaybar will prevail."

al-Hajjaj ibn 'Ilat al-Sulami (al-Hajjaj ibn 'Ilat) had embraced Islam and witnessed the conquest of Khaybar. He was married to Umm Shayba, a sister of the Banu 'Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy, and al-Hajjaj was a man of great wealth. He had mines in the land of the Banu Sulaym. When the Prophet ﷺ gained victory over Khaybar, al-Hajjaj ibn 'Ilat said, "I have gold with my wife. If she and her family learn of my Islam, I will have no wealth. So permit me to hasten on my journey and outpace the news, and I will spread reports that will help me protect my wealth and my person when I arrive." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ permitted him.

When he came to Makkah, he said to his wife, "Hide from me and gather whatever wealth I have with you, for I want to buy some of the spoils of Muhammad and his companions, for they have been plundered and their wealth has been taken. Muhammad has been taken captive, his companions have scattered from him, and the Jews have sworn that they will send him to Makkah and then kill him in retaliation for their dead in Madinah." This spread in Makkah, and it weighed heavily upon the Muslims and affected them greatly, while the polytheists openly showed joy and delight.

Al-'Abbas, the paternal uncle of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, heard the uproar of the people, their clamour, and their display of delight. He wanted to stand up and go out, but his back gave way and he could not rise. He called a son of his named Qutham, who resembled the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and al-'Abbas began to recite rhyming verses in a raised voice, so that the enemies of Allah would not gloat over him:

"My beloved Qutham, my beloved Qutham,
resembler of the one with the lofty nose,
the Prophet of my Lord, the possessor of blessings,
in spite of the nose of whoever is humiliated."

Many men, both Muslims and polytheists, gathered at the door of his house. Among them were those who openly showed joy and delight, among them the one who gloated and incited, and among them those who were as if struck by death from grief and affliction. When the Muslims heard al-'Abbas's verses and his composure, their hearts were eased, and the polytheists thought that a misfortune had befallen him that had not befallen them.

Then al-'Abbas sent a slave of his to al-Hajjaj and said to him, "Get him alone and say to him: Woe to you! What have you brought, and what are you saying? What Allah has promised is better than what you have brought." When the slave spoke with him, al-Hajjaj said, "Convey my greetings to Abu al-Fadl and say to him: Let him meet me alone in some of his rooms until I come to him, for the news is what will gladden him." When the slave reached the door of the house, he said, "Good news, O Abu al-Fadl!" Al-'Abbas leapt up joyfully, as if no affliction had ever touched him, until he reached him, and kissed him between the eyes. He informed him of al-Hajjaj's words, and al-'Abbas freed him. Then he said, "Tell me more." The slave said, "al-Hajjaj says to you: Meet him alone in some of your rooms until he comes to you at midday."

When al-Hajjaj came to him and they were alone, al-'Abbas took an oath from him: "You must keep my news secret." Al-Hajjaj agreed to this, and al-'Abbas said to him, "I have come, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has conquered Khaybar and seized their wealth. The arrows of Allah have run through it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has chosen Safiyya bint Huyayy for himself and consummated the marriage with her. But I came for my wealth, wanting to gather it and take it away. I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission to speak, and he permitted me to say whatever I wished. So keep this secret from me for three days, and then mention whatever you wish."

He said: His wife gathered his belongings for him, and then he set off back. When three days had passed, al-'Abbas came to al-Hajjaj's wife and said, "What has your husband done?" She said, "He has gone." She also said, "May Allah not grieve you, O Abu al-Fadl. What has reached you has grieved us greatly." He said, "Indeed, may Allah not grieve me. By the praise of Allah, there was nothing but what I love. Allah granted His Messenger victory at Khaybar, the arrows of Allah ran through it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ chose Safiyya for himself. So if you have any need for your husband, then go to him." She said, "I think you are truthful, by Allah." He said, "By Allah, I am truthful, and the matter is as I tell you." She said, "Who informed you of this?" He said, "The One who informed you of what He informed you."

Then he went until he came to the gatherings of the Quraysh. When they saw him they said, "By Allah, this is composure, O Abu al-Fadl, and nothing but good will touch you." He said, "Indeed, nothing but good has touched me, and praise be to Allah. al-Hajjaj informed me of such and such, and he asked me to keep it secret from him for three days for a need." Thus Allah turned the grief and anxiety that the Muslims had felt into distress for the polytheists. The Muslims left their places until they came to al-'Abbas, and he told them the news, and the faces of the Muslims shone with joy.

He promised them many spoils that they would take, and informed them that He had hastened this spoil for them.

There are two opinions about it. The first is that it refers to the truce that took place between them and their enemy. The second is that it refers to the conquest of Khaybar and its spoils.

Then He said: ﴿And He restrained the hands of the people from you﴾.

It was said: the hands of the people of Makkah, that they should fight them.

It was also said: the hands of the Jews, when they intended to assassinate those in Madinah after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had left it with those of the Companions who were with him. It was also said: they are the people of Khaybar and their allies who wanted to help them, from Asad and Ghatafan. The sound view is that the verse includes all of them.

As for His saying: ﴿And that it may be a sign for the believers﴾:

It was said: this act which He performed for you, namely restraining the hands of your enemies from you despite their great number, since at that time the people of Makkah and those around it, the people of Khaybar and those around it, Asad, Ghatafan, and most of the tribes of the Arabs were enemies to them, and they were among them like a mole on the skin (*al-shamah*). Yet they did not reach them with any harm. So among the signs of Allah, glorified is He, is the restraining of their enemies' hands from them, so that they did not reach them with harm despite their great number and the severity of their hostility, and His taking charge of guarding and protecting them whether they were present or absent.

It was also said: it refers to the conquest of Khaybar, which He made a sign for His believing servants and a token of what would follow it of conquests. For Allah, glorified is He, had promised them many spoils and great conquests, so He hastened for them the conquest of Khaybar, and made it a sign of what would follow it, and a reward for their patience and contentment on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah, and a thanks. For this reason He specified it, and its spoils, for those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyyah.

Then He said: ﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾.

So He combined for them, along with victory, triumph and spoils, guidance. He made them guided, victorious, and gaining spoils. Then He promised them many spoils and other conquests which they were not yet able to attain at that time. It was said: these are Makkah; it was said: they are Persia and Rome.

It was also said: the conquests that came after Khaybar are from the eastern and western parts of the earth.

[Section: On the Expedition of Khaybar]

Musa ibn ʿUqbah said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to Madinah from al-Hudaybiyyah, he stayed there about twenty nights or close to that, then he set out as a raider towards Khaybar. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had promised him it while he was at al-Hudaybiyyah.

Malik said: the conquest of Khaybar took place in the sixth year, but the majority hold that it was in the seventh.

Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm asserted that it was in the sixth year without doubt. Perhaps the disagreement is based on the starting point of the calendar: is it the month of Rabiʿ al-Awwal, the month of his arrival in Madinah, or Muharram at the beginning of the year? People have two approaches to this:

The majority hold that the calendar began with Muharram, while Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm holds that it began with Rabiʿ al-Awwal, when he arrived. (The first to date by the Hijrah was Yaʿla ibn Umayyah in Yemen), as Imam Ahmad narrated it with a sound chain.

It was also said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, in the sixteenth year of the Hijrah.

Ibn Ishaq said: al-Zuhri narrated to me from ʿUrwah, from Marwan ibn al-Hakam and al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, that both of them narrated to him, saying: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, and the Surah of Victory (al-Fath) was revealed to him between Makkah and Madinah, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave him Khaybar through it, ﴿Allah has promised you many spoils that you will take, and has hastened this for you﴾ [al-Fath: 20], which is Khaybar. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah in Dhu al-Hijjah, and stayed there until he set out for Khaybar in Muharram. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ halted at al-Raji', a valley between Khaybar and Ghatafan, and feared that Ghatafan would support them, so he spent the night there until morning, then set out towards them. End of quote.

He appointed Siba' ibn ʿUrfutah as his deputy over Madinah. Abu Hurayrah arrived in Madinah at that time and met Siba' ibn ʿUrfutah at the dawn prayer, and he heard him recite in the first rak'ah: *Kaf-Ha-Ya-ʿAyn-Sad*, and in the second: *Woe to those who give less* (al-Mutaffifin). So he said to himself: Woe to so-and-so, he has two measures: when he takes by measure he takes in full, and when he gives by measure he gives short. When he had finished his prayer, he went to Siba' and provided him, until he reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and spoke to the Muslims, and they included him and his companions in their shares.

Salamah ibn al-Akwa' said: "We set out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ towards Khaybar, and we travelled by night. A man from the people said to ʿAmir ibn al-Akwaʿ: Will you not make us hear some of your verses?

ʿAmir was a poet, so he dismounted and began to drive the camels for the people, saying:

*O Allah, had it not been for You, we would not have been guided,*
*nor would we have given charity or prayed.*
*So forgive, as a ransom for You, what we have committed,*
*and make our feet firm if we meet [the enemy].*
*And send down tranquillity upon us,*
*for when a cry is raised against us, we come.*
*They sought to overwhelm us with the cry,*
*but if they desire strife, we refuse.*

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Who is this driver?" They said: ʿAmir. He said: "May Allah have mercy on him." A man from the people said: "He has become a martyr (*wajibat*), O Messenger of Allah! Why did you not let us benefit from him?" He said: So we came to Khaybar and besieged them until severe hunger afflicted us. Then Allah, Exalted is He, granted us victory over them. When evening came, they lit many fires. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What are these fires? On what are you lighting them?"

They said: "On meat."

He said: "On what meat?"

They said: "On the meat of domestic donkeys."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Spill it and break the pots." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we spill it and wash them?" He said: "Or that?"

When the two sides lined up, Marhab came out swaggering with his sword, saying:

*Khaybar knows that I am Marhab,*
*armed, a brave and experienced warrior,*
*when the wars come blazing.*

ʿAmir came down to him saying:

*Khaybar knows that I am ʿAmir,*
*armed, a brave warrior who plunges in.*

They exchanged two blows. Marhab's sword struck the shield of ʿAmir, and ʿAmir moved to strike him from below, but his sword was short, so its edge turned back upon him and struck the knee-joint, and he died from it. Salamah said to the Prophet ﷺ: "They claim that ʿAmir's deeds have been nullified." He said: "The one who said that is a liar. He has two rewards," and he joined his two fingers together, "he is truly a striver and a fighter. Few Arabs have walked with it as he did."

[Section: On the Arrival at Khaybar]

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived at Khaybar, he prayed the dawn prayer there, and the Muslims mounted up. The people of Khaybar came out with their hoes and baskets, not realising, for they had gone out to their lands. When they saw the army, they said: "Muhammad, by Allah! Muhammad and the army!" Then they returned fleeing to their fortresses. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah is greatest, Khaybar is ruined! Allah is greatest, Khaybar is ruined! When we descend into the courtyard of a people, the morning of those who were warned is evil."

When the Prophet ﷺ drew near and overlooked it, he said: "Halt." The army halted, and he said:

"O Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and what they overshadow, and Lord of the seven earths and what they carry, and Lord of the devils and what they lead astray. We ask You for the good of this town, the good of its people, and the good of what is in it, and we seek refuge in You from the evil of this town, the evil of its people, and the evil of what is in it. Advance in the name of Allah."

On the night of the entry, he said: "I will surely give this banner tomorrow to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love; Allah will grant victory through his hands." The people spent the night discussing among themselves which of them would be given it. When morning came, the people all went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ hoping to be given it. He said: "Where is ʿAli ibn Abi Talib?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, he has an eye complaint." He said: "Send for him."

He was brought, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spat in his eyes and prayed for him, and he was healed as though he had never had any pain. He gave him the banner. ʿAli said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I fight them until they become like us?" He said: "Proceed calmly until you alight in their courtyard, then call them to Islam, and inform them of what is incumbent upon them of Allah's right in it. By Allah, for Allah to guide one man through you is better for you than red camels."

Marhab came out saying:

*I am the one whom my mother named Marhab,*
*armed, a brave and experienced warrior,*
*when the wars come blazing.*

ʿAli came out to him saying:

*I am the one whom my mother named Haydarah,*
*like a lion of thickets, of fearsome appearance,*
*I give them full measure, like the sandara measure.*

He struck Marhab and split his skull, and that was the conquest.

When ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, drew near their fortresses, a Jew looked out from the top of the fortress and said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am ʿAli ibn Abi Talib." The Jew said: "You have prevailed, but what was sent down to Musa was not..." [the Jew said this in mockery, meaning: you have overcome, but the Torah was not given to you].

This is how it is in *Sahih Muslim* that "ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, is the one who killed Marhab." Musa ibn ʿUqbah said, on the authority of al-Zuhri and Abu al-Aswad, from ʿUrwah; and Yunus ibn Bukayr, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Sahl, one of the Banu Harithah, narrated to me, on the authority of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, that Muhammad ibn Maslamah was the one who killed him." Jabir said in his narration: "Marhab the Jew came out of the fortress of Khaybar, having gathered his weapons, and he was chanting verse and saying: Who will duel? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Who will deal with this? Muhammad ibn Maslamah said: I will, O Messenger of Allah. By Allah, I am the one who seeks vengeance and avenges, they killed my brother yesterday," meaning Mahmud ibn Maslamah, who had been killed at Khaybar. He said: "Go out to him, O Allah, help him against him." When each of them drew close to the other, a tree came between them, and each of them took cover behind it from the other. Whenever one took cover behind it from the other, the other cut away what was in front of him from it with his sword, until each of them came out facing the other, and between them the tree became like a standing man with no branches on it. Then he (Marhab) charged at Muhammad and struck him, but he guarded himself with the shield, and his sword became stuck in it, and it clamped down on it and held it. Then Muhammad ibn Maslamah struck him and killed him." Likewise, Salamah ibn Salamah and Majmaʿ ibn Harithah said that Muhammad ibn Maslamah killed Marhab.

Al-Waqidi said: It was also said: "Muhammad ibn Maslamah struck the two legs of Marhab and cut them off, and Marhab said: Finish me off, O Muhammad. Muhammad said: Taste death as my brother Mahmud tasted it." He passed by him, and ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, passed by him, struck his neck and took his spoils. They disputed before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over his spoils. Muhammad ibn Maslamah said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not cut off his legs and leave him except so that he might taste death, and I was able to finish him off." ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "He has spoken the truth. I struck his neck after he had cut off his legs." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave Muhammad ibn Maslamah his sword, spear, helmet and shield.

The sword of Marhab was among the family of Muhammad ibn Maslamah, and in it was a writing that no one knew the meaning of, until a Jew read it, and in it was:

*This is the sword of Marhab;*
*whoever tastes it will perish.*

Then, after Marhab, his brother Yasir came out, and al-Zubayr came out against him. Safiyyah, his mother, said: "O Messenger of Allah, is he going to kill my son?" He said: "Rather, your son will kill him, if Allah wills." Then al-Zubayr killed him.

Musa ibn ʿUqbah said: Then the Jews entered a fortress of theirs that was impregnable, called al-Qamus. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ besieged them for about twenty nights. It was a pestilential land of severe heat, and the Muslims suffered greatly. They slaughtered the donkeys, but the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade them from eating them. A black Abyssinian slave from the people of Khaybar, who had been tending sheep for his master, came. When he saw the people of Khaybar had taken up weapons, he asked them: "What do you want?"

They said: "We will fight this man who claims to be a prophet." Thoughts of the Prophet ﷺ came into his heart. He came with his sheep to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "What do you say, and what do you call to?" He said: "I call to Islam, and that you testify that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah, and that you worship none but Allah."

The slave said: "What do I gain if I testify and believe in Allah, Mighty and Majestic?" He said: "Paradise for you, if you die upon that."

He took Islam and then said, "O Messenger of God, these sheep are a trust I hold." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him, "Take them out from your possession and throw pebbles at them, for God will discharge your trust on your behalf." He did so, and the sheep returned to their owner. The Jew then knew that his slave had embraced Islam.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood among the people, admonished them, and urged them to jihad (striving in the way of God, including armed fighting). When the Muslims and the Jews met in battle, among those killed was the black slave. The Muslims carried him to their encampment, and he was placed in the fustat (a tent). They reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) looked into the tent, then turned to his companions and said: "God has honoured this slave and led him to good. I saw by his head two of the wide-eyed houris, and he never once prostrated to God."

Hammad ibn Salamah said, on the authority of Thabit, from Anas: "A man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said, 'O Messenger of God, I am a man of black complexion, ugly of face, foul of smell, and I have no wealth. If I fight these people until I am killed, will I enter Paradise?' He said, 'Yes.'

So he advanced, fought until he was killed. The Prophet (ﷺ) came upon him while he was slain and said, 'God has beautified your face, perfumed your scent, and multiplied your wealth.' Then he said, 'I saw his two wives from the wide-eyed houris pulling off his robe, entering between his skin and his robe.'"

Shaddad ibn al-Hadi said: "A man from the Bedouin came to the Prophet (ﷺ), believed in him and followed him, and said, 'I will migrate with you.' So he (the Prophet) entrusted him to some of his companions. When the expedition of Khaybar came, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took some booty and divided it, and he set aside a share for the Bedouin. His companions gave him what had been set aside for him, and he was tending their animals. When he came, they handed it to him. He said, 'What is this?' They said, 'A share the Messenger of God (ﷺ) set aside for you.' He took it and came with it to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, 'What is this, O Messenger of God?' He said, 'A share I set aside for you.' He said, 'It was not on this basis that I followed you; rather, I followed you on condition that I be struck here,' and he pointed to his throat, 'by an arrow, so that I die and enter Paradise.' He (the Prophet) said, 'If you are truthful to God, He will be truthful to you.' Then he rose to fight the enemy, and he was brought to the Prophet (ﷺ) while slain. He said, 'Is it him?' They said, 'Yes.' He said, 'He was truthful to God, so God has been truthful to him.' The Prophet (ﷺ) shrouded him in his own robe, then put him forward and prayed over him. Among his supplications for him was: 'O God, this is Your servant who went out as a migrant in Your way; he was killed as a martyr, and I am a witness to it.'"

Al-Waqidi said: "The Jews moved to the fortress of al-Zubayr, a strong stronghold on the top of a hill. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) stayed there three days. A Jewish man called Azal came and said, 'O Abu al-Qasim, even if you remained for a month, they would not care. They have a water supply and springs beneath the earth; they come out at night, drink from them, then return to their fortress and hold out against you. If you cut off their water supply, they will come out to you.' So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) marched to their water, cut it off from them. When it was cut off, they came out and fought the fiercest fight. Some of the Muslims were killed, and about ten Jews were struck down. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) conquered it. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) moved to the people of al-Kutaybah, al-Watih and al-Salalim, the fortress of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq. Its people fortified themselves most strongly, and every fugitive who had fled from al-Natat and al-Shiqq came to them. Khaybar had two parts: the first was al-Shiqq and al-Natat, which he had conquered first; the second part was al-Kutaybah, al-Watih and al-Salalim. They would not come out from their fortresses until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) intended to set up the mangonel against them. When they became certain of destruction, after the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had besieged them for fourteen days, they asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for peace. Ibn Abi al-Huqayq sent to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'Shall I come down and speak with you?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, 'Yes.' Ibn Abi al-Huqayq came down and made peace with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on condition that the blood of those among them who were fighting men in their fortresses be spared, and that the children be left to them, and that they leave Khaybar and its land with their offspring, and that they leave the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in possession of whatever wealth and land they had, along with the gold, the silver, the weapons and the armour, except for a garment on a person's back. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'The protection of God and the protection of His Messenger is withdrawn from you if you conceal anything from me.' They made peace with him on that basis."

Hammad ibn Salamah said: Ubayd Allah ibn Umar informed us, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) fought the people of Khaybar until he drove them into their castle, and he took control of the crops, the palm trees and the land. They made peace with him on condition that they be expelled from it, and that they keep whatever their mounts could carry, while the gold and silver belonged to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He stipulated that they must not conceal or hide anything, and if they did, they would have no protection and no covenant. They then hid a leather bag containing wealth and jewelry belonging to Huyayy ibn Akhtab, which he had brought with him to Khaybar when al-Nadir were expelled. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to the paternal uncle of Huyayy ibn Akhtab: 'What became of the leather bag of Huyayy which he brought from al-Nadir?' He said: 'Expenses and wars have consumed it.' He said: 'The covenant is recent, and the wealth is more than that.' So he handed him over to al-Zubayr, who tormented him. Before this, Huyayy had entered a ruin and said: 'I have seen Huyayy circling in a ruin here.' They went and searched, and found the bag in the ruin. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) then killed the two sons of Abu al-Huqayq, one of whom was the husband of Safiyyah bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) took captive their women and children, and divided their property, because of the breach of covenant they had committed. He intended to expel them from it, but they said: 'O Muhammad, let us remain in this land, to cultivate it and tend it, for we know it better than you.'

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions had no servants to tend it, and they could not devote themselves to tending it. So he gave them Khaybar on condition that they receive half of every crop and every fruit, for as long as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wished to let them remain. Abd Allah ibn Rawahah used to estimate its produce for them, as has been mentioned earlier. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not kill anyone after the peace except the two sons of Abu al-Huqayq, because of the breach of covenant they had committed; for they had stipulated that if they concealed or hid anything, the protection of God and of His Messenger would be withdrawn from them. They hid something, so he said to them: 'Where is the wealth you took out of Madinah when we expelled you?' They said: 'It is gone.' They swore to that, but the cousin of Kinanah admitted to the wealth against the two of them, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) handed him over to al-Zubayr to torment him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) then handed Kinanah over to Muhammad ibn Maslamah, who killed him." It is said that Kinanah was the one who had killed the brother of Mahmud ibn Maslamah.

"The Messenger of God (ﷺ) took captive Safiyyah bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab and the daughter of her paternal aunt. Safiyyah had been married to Kinanah ibn Abi al-Huqayq, and she was a recent bride who had only just consummated the marriage. He ordered Bilal to take her to his camp, and Bilal passed by her amid the slain. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) disliked that and said: 'Has mercy been removed from you, O Bilal?!'"

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) offered her Islam, and she embraced it. He chose her for himself, freed her, and made her freedom her bridal gift. He consummated the marriage with her on the way and held a wedding feast for her. He noticed a greenish mark on her face and said: "What is this?" She said: "O Messenger of God, before you came to us, I saw in a dream that the moon had moved from its place and fallen into my lap. By God, I do not remember anything else about you." She recounted it to her husband, and he slapped her face and said: "You long for this king who is in Madinah!"

The Companions doubted whether he had taken her as a concubine or as a wife. They said: "Look: if he veils her, then she is one of his wives; otherwise she is among those whom his right hand owns." When he mounted, he placed his garment over her back and face, then tied its end beneath her. They then held back from him on the journey, and knew that she was one of his wives. When he came to lift her onto the mount, she out of reverence for him avoided placing her foot on his thigh, so she placed her knee on his thigh, then rode.

When he had consummated the marriage with her, Abu Ayyub spent the night standing near his tent, holding the hilt of his sword until morning. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came out and Abu Ayyub saw him, he exclaimed "Allahu akbar" upon seeing him come out. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked him: "What is wrong with you, Abu Ayyub?" He said: "O Messenger of God, I could not sleep last night when you entered upon this woman. I remembered that you had killed her father, her brother, her husband and most of her clan, so I feared that she might assassinate you." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) laughed and said something kind to him.

[The story of a Jewish woman poisoning the Prophet (ﷺ)]

During this campaign, "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was poisoned. Zaynab bint al-Harith, the Jewess, wife of Sallam ibn Mishkam, presented him with a roasted sheep that she had poisoned. She asked: 'Which meat does he love most?' They said: 'The foreleg.' So she put a great deal of poison in the foreleg. When he bit into its meat, the foreleg informed him that it was poisoned. He spat out the morsel, then said: 'Gather for me all the Jews who are here.' They were gathered for him, and he said to them: 'I am going to ask you about something; will you be truthful with me about it?' They said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'Who is your father?' They said: 'Our father is so-and-so.' He said: 'You lie; your father is so-and-so.' They said: 'You have spoken the truth and done good.' He said: 'Will you be truthful with me about something if I ask you about it?' They said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim, and if we lie to you, you will recognise our lie just as you recognised it concerning our father.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Who are the people of the Fire?' They said: 'We will remain in it for a short time, and then you will succeed us in it.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'Be silent and remain there; by God, we will never succeed you in it, ever.'

Then he said: 'Will you be truthful with me about something if I ask you about it?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Did you put poison in this sheep?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What led you to do that?' They said: 'We intended, if you were a liar, that we would be rid of you; and if you were a prophet, it would not harm you.'"

"The woman was brought to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and she said: 'I intended to kill you.' He said: 'God would not have empowered you over me.' They said: 'Shall we not kill her?' He said: 'No.' He did not hold her to account and did not punish her." He had himself cupped on the shoulder blade, and he ordered those who had eaten from it to be cupped, and some of them died. There was disagreement about whether the woman was killed. Al-Zuhri said: "She embraced Islam, so he left her alone." Abd al-Razzaq reported this from Ma'mar from him. Then Ma'mar said: "The people say the Prophet (ﷺ) killed her."

Abu Dawud said: Wahb ibn Baqiyyah narrated to us, saying: Khalid narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Amr, from Abu Salamah, that "a Jewish woman in Khaybar presented the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a roasted sheep." He mentioned the story and said: "Bishr ibn al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur died, so he sent to the Jewish woman: 'What led you to do what you did?'" Jabir said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered her to be brought, and she was killed."

I say: both reports are mursal (lacking a companion in the chain). Hammad ibn Salamah related it from Muhammad ibn Amr, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, in a connected form, that he killed her when Bishr ibn al-Bara' died.

The two reports have been reconciled by saying that he did not kill her at first, but when Bishr died, he killed her.

There is disagreement as to whether the Prophet (ﷺ) ate from it or did not eat. Most reports say that he ate from it, and he remained after that for three years, until in the illness in which he died he said: "I have continued to feel the effect of the morsel I ate from the sheep on the day of Khaybar; this is the time of the severing of my aorta."

Al-Zuhri said: "So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) died as a martyr."

Musa ibn 'Uqba and others said: When the Quraysh heard that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had set out for Khaybar, there was a great dispute and wagering among them. Some said, "Muhammad and his companions will prevail." Others said, "The two allies and the Jews of Khaybar will prevail."

al-Hajjaj ibn 'Ilat al-Sulami (al-Hajjaj ibn 'Ilat) had embraced Islam and witnessed the conquest of Khaybar. He was married to Umm Shayba, a sister of the Banu 'Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy, and al-Hajjaj was a man of great wealth. He had mines in the land of the Banu Sulaym. When the Prophet ﷺ gained victory over Khaybar, al-Hajjaj ibn 'Ilat said, "I have gold with my wife. If she and her family learn of my Islam, I will have no wealth. So permit me to hasten on my journey and outpace the news, and I will spread reports that will help me protect my wealth and my person when I arrive." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ permitted him.

When he came to Makkah, he said to his wife, "Hide from me and gather whatever wealth I have with you, for I want to buy some of the spoils of Muhammad and his companions, for they have been plundered and their wealth has been taken. Muhammad has been taken captive, his companions have scattered from him, and the Jews have sworn that they will send him to Makkah and then kill him in retaliation for their dead in Madinah." This spread in Makkah, and it weighed heavily upon the Muslims and affected them greatly, while the polytheists openly showed joy and delight.

Al-'Abbas, the paternal uncle of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, heard the uproar of the people, their clamour, and their display of delight. He wanted to stand up and go out, but his back gave way and he could not rise. He called a son of his named Qutham, who resembled the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and al-'Abbas began to recite rhyming verses in a raised voice, so that the enemies of Allah would not gloat over him:

"My beloved Qutham, my beloved Qutham,
resembler of the one with the lofty nose,
the Prophet of my Lord, the possessor of blessings,
in spite of the nose of whoever is humiliated."

Many men, both Muslims and polytheists, gathered at the door of his house. Among them were those who openly showed joy and delight, among them the one who gloated and incited, and among them those who were as if struck by death from grief and affliction. When the Muslims heard al-'Abbas's verses and his composure, their hearts were eased, and the polytheists thought that a misfortune had befallen him that had not befallen them.

Then al-'Abbas sent a slave of his to al-Hajjaj and said to him, "Get him alone and say to him: Woe to you! What have you brought, and what are you saying? What Allah has promised is better than what you have brought." When the slave spoke with him, al-Hajjaj said, "Convey my greetings to Abu al-Fadl and say to him: Let him meet me alone in some of his rooms until I come to him, for the news is what will gladden him."
