When the slave reached the door of the house, he said, "Good news, O Abu al-Fadl!" Al-'Abbas leapt up joyfully, as if no affliction had ever touched him, until he reached him, and kissed him between the eyes. He informed him of al-Hajjaj's words, and al-'Abbas freed him. Then he said, "Tell me more." The slave said, "al-Hajjaj says to you: Meet him alone in some of your rooms until he comes to you at midday."

When al-Hajjaj came to him and they were alone, al-'Abbas took an oath from him: "You must keep my news secret." Al-Hajjaj agreed to this, and al-'Abbas said to him, "I have come, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has conquered Khaybar and seized their wealth. The arrows of Allah have run through it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has chosen Safiyya bint Huyayy for himself and consummated the marriage with her. But I came for my wealth, wanting to gather it and take it away. I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission to speak, and he permitted me to say whatever I wished. So keep this secret from me for three days, and then mention whatever you wish."

He said: His wife gathered his belongings for him, and then he set off back. When three days had passed, al-'Abbas came to al-Hajjaj's wife and said, "What has your husband done?" She said, "He has gone." She also said, "May Allah not grieve you, O Abu al-Fadl. What has reached you has grieved us greatly." He said, "Indeed, may Allah not grieve me. By the praise of Allah, there was nothing but what I love. Allah granted His Messenger victory at Khaybar, the arrows of Allah ran through it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ chose Safiyya for himself. So if you have any need for your husband, then go to him." She said, "I think you are truthful, by Allah." He said, "By Allah, I am truthful, and the matter is as I tell you." She said, "Who informed you of this?" He said, "The One who informed you of what He informed you."

Then he went until he came to the gatherings of the Quraysh. When they saw him they said, "By Allah, this is composure, O Abu al-Fadl, and nothing but good will touch you." He said, "Indeed, nothing but good has touched me, and praise be to Allah. al-Hajjaj informed me of such and such, and he asked me to keep it secret from him for three days for a need." Thus Allah turned the grief and anxiety that the Muslims had felt into distress for the polytheists. The Muslims left their places until they came to al-'Abbas, and he told them the news, and the faces of the Muslims shone with joy.

Allah, glory be to Him, informed that if the disbelievers were to fight His allies, the disbelievers would turn their backs in flight, not being helped. And that this is His practice with His servants before them, and there is no change in His practice.

If it is said: They fought them on the Day of Uhud and overcame them, and did not turn their backs?

It is said: This is a promise conditioned on a condition mentioned in another place, namely patience (al-sabr) and piety (al-taqwa). This condition was lost on the Day of Uhud through their cowardice (fashal), which contradicts patience, and their dispute (tanazu') and disobedience (isyan), which contradict piety. So He turned them away from their enemy, and the promise was not fulfilled because its condition was absent.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about what the disbelievers had placed in their hearts of the zealotry of ignorance (ḥamiyyat al-jāhiliyya), whose source is ignorance and wrongdoing, and for which they barred His Messenger and His servants from His House. They did not acknowledge ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, and they did not acknowledge to Muhammad that he is the Messenger of Allah, though they were certain of his truthfulness and sure of the soundness of his message through the proofs they had witnessed and heard during a period of twenty years. He attributed this placing to them, though it was by His decree and destiny, just as all their actions are attributed to them, which are by their power and will.

Then He, glorified is He, informed that He sent down into the heart of His Messenger and his allies a tranquillity (sakīna) that corresponds to what is in the hearts of their enemies of the zealotry of ignorance. Thus tranquillity was the portion of His Messenger and his party, and the zealotry of ignorance was the portion of the polytheists and their army. Then He obligated His believing servants to the word of piety (kalimat al-taqwā), which is a genus encompassing every word by which Allah is feared, and its highest kind is the word of sincerity (kalimat al-ikhlāṣ). It has been explained as ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, and it is the word that Quraysh refused to adhere to. So Allah obligated it upon His allies and His party, and He deprived His enemies of it only to preserve it from those who are not its equals, and He obligated it upon the one who is more worthy of it and its people. He placed it in its proper place and did not waste it by placing it with those who are not its people, and He is the All-Knowing of the places of His distinction and its positions.

[Section: The Difference Between Ḥamiyya and Jafā’]

Likewise is the difference between ḥamiyya and jafā’. Ḥamiyya is the weaning of the soul from suckling blame from a breast that is the outlet of vices, base qualities and lowly things, even if its milk is abundant and people crowd upon it. For them there is a weaning, with which hearts are severed in sorrow, so weaning is necessary. If you hasten, you are praiseworthy and thanked; and if you delay, you are not rewarded.

Unlike jafā’, which is a harshness in the soul, hardness in the heart and density in the nature, from which arises a disposition called jafā’.

(Section)

The word of piety is the word by which Allah is feared, and the highest kind of this word is the saying "There is no god but Allah." Then every word by which Allah is feared after it is from the word of piety.

He, glorified is He, has informed that He obligated it upon the believing servants, making it binding upon them so that they do not part from it. By His obligating it, they committed to it; were it not for His obligating it upon them, they would not have committed to it. Its commitment is a voluntary act following their will and choice; He is the one who obligates and they are the ones who commit.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And He made them adhere to the word of piety, and they were more worthy of it and its people﴾

(Principle)

The testimony that there is no god but Allah at the time of death has a great effect in expiating sins and nullifying them, because it is the testimony of a servant who is certain of it, knows its meaning, whose desires have died within him, whose rebellious soul has softened and submitted after its refusal and disobedience, has turned back after its aversion, has been humbled after its pride, has departed from greed for this world and its excess, and has been abased before its Lord, its Creator and its true Master, at its most humbled and most hopeful for His pardon, forgiveness and mercy. Through it, monotheism is stripped bare by the severing of the causes of shirk and the realization of its falsehood. Thereby those disputes which had occupied it are removed, and its concern gathers upon the One whom it is certain it will meet and to whom it will return. The servant turns his whole face to Him, and turns his heart, spirit and concern toward Him; he submits to Him alone, outwardly and inwardly, and his secret and public are equal. So he says, "There is no god but Allah," sincerely from his heart, and his heart has been freed from attachment to other than Him and from turning to anything besides Him. The whole world has departed from his heart, he is about to meet his Lord, the fires of his desire have died down, and his heart is filled with the Hereafter, so that it becomes before his eyes, and the world becomes behind his back. That pure testimony becomes the seal of his deeds, purifying him from his sins and bringing him in before his Lord, because he meets his Lord with a true and pure testimony whose outward matches its inward, and whose secret matches its public. Had this testimony been attained in this manner during times of health, he would have felt estranged from the world and its people, fled to Allah from people, and found intimacy in Him alone. But he bore witness to it with a heart filled with desires and love of life and its means, and a soul filled with pursuing pleasures and turning to other than Allah. Had it been stripped bare as it is at death, it would have had another report and another life, apart from its animal life. And Allah is the One whose help is sought.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 48, verse 27:

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed that He had made true His Messenger's vision of entering the Sacred Mosque in security, and that it would surely come to pass, but the time for it had not yet arrived in that year. Allah, glorified is He, knew of the benefit in delaying it until its appointed time what you did not know. You loved to hasten it, whereas the Lord, exalted is He, knows of the benefit and wisdom in the delay what you did not know. So He sent before it a near victory as a preparation for it and a paving of the way.

(Section)

Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, related from the narration of Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Zayd that his father told him that he witnessed the Prophet ﷺ at the place of sacrifice, and a man from Quraysh was distributing sacrificial animals, but he did not receive anything, nor did his companion. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ shaved his head in his garment, and gave it to him, and he distributed it among men, and he trimmed his nails and gave them to his companion. He said: "Indeed, it is dyed with henna and katam (indigo) among us," meaning his hair.

He invoked forgiveness three times for those who shaved, and once for those who trimmed. Many of the Companions shaved, indeed most of them, and some of them trimmed. This is along with the words of the Most High: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security, with your heads shaved and [some] hair cut short﴾ [al-Fath: 27].

And along with the statement of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "I perfumed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for his ihram before he entered ihram, and for his release (from ihram) before he was released," which is evidence that shaving is an act of worship (nusuk) and not merely the lifting of a prohibition.

(Benefit)

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq was the most understanding of the Ummah of the words of Allah and His Messenger. For this reason, when the verse ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ became difficult for Umar despite the strength of his understanding,

and the Prophet ﷺ's saying to the Companions: "You will come to it and circumambulate it,"

he raised it against him in the year of Hudaybiyah, and al-Siddiq said to him: "Did he tell you that you would come to it this year?"

He said: No.

He said: "Then you will come to it and circumambulate it."

So he answered him with the answer of the Prophet ﷺ.

Also difficult for him was the fighting of Abu Bakr against those who withheld zakat, although the Prophet ﷺ had said: "I have been commanded to fight people until they say, 'There is no god but Allah.' When they say it, they have protected their blood and their property from me."

Umar said: Did he not say "except for its right"? And giving zakat is part of its right.

When the Prophet ﷺ informed them: "Indeed a servant was given the choice by Allah between this world and what is with Him, and he chose what is with Allah," Abu Bakr wept and said: "We ransom you with our sons and our mothers." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the one given the choice, and Abu Bakr was the most knowledgeable of the Ummah about him.

(Section)

The words of the Most High: ﴿Allah had certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security, with your heads shaved and [some] hair cut short, fearing none. He knew what you did not know, and He made, besides that, a near victory﴾

He, glorified is He, explained the wisdom in what they disliked in the year of Hudaybiyah, namely the prevention by the polytheists of them, until they returned without performing ʿumrah. He made clear to them that their goal would be attained after this, and it was attained in the following year. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿He knew what you did not know and made, besides that, a near victory﴾

This is the treaty of Hudaybiyah, and it is the first of the victory mentioned in His words: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾

For by means of it there came about, of the benefits of religion and worldly life, victory, the rise of Islam, and the defeat of disbelief, what they had not been hoping for before. People mingled with one another, Muslims spoke the word of Islam and its proofs and evidences openly, without fear. At that time, many more entered Islam than had entered it up to that point. The transgression, enmity, and obstinacy of the polytheists became manifest to everyone, and both the elite and the common people knew that Muhammad and his Companions had the rightful claim and guidance, and that their enemies had nothing in their hands but aggression and obstinacy. The Sacred House had not been barred to any pilgrim or ʿumrah performer since the time of Abraham, so the Arabs became certain of the obstinacy and enmity of Quraysh. This became a call for many people to Islam, while the obstinacy and tyranny of that people increased, and this was among the greatest aids against themselves. The patience and endurance of the believers increased, and their adherence to Allah's command and obedience to His Messenger, and this is among the greatest causes of their victory, along with other matters that Allah knew and the Companions did not know. For this reason He called it a victory. The Prophet ﷺ was asked: "Was it a victory?" He said: "Yes."

(Benefit)

The verb occurring after the conditional particle is sometimes intended and relied upon, so it is the object of the conditional clause, and the apodosis is made a means and instrument to achieve it.

In this context, the use of the imperfect (muḍāriʿ) verb, indicating that the intention is that he will perform it and bring it about, is emphasized or required. The manifest intention toward it required the verbal action to take effect upon it, so that the wording matches the meaning, and the verbal and the semantic effects combine.

What indicates this is that they reversed the form of the past verb into the future in the conditional for this meaning, so that the effect of the condition and its requirement on it would appear.

When the speech relies on the apodosis and the intention toward it, and the condition is made subordinate and a means to it, using the past form is good, or better than the future. So weigh by this rule whatever objections arise to you in this section.

Among them is the words of the Most High: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾

Observe how He made the conditional verb past and the apodosis future, because the intention was toward their entering the Sacred Mosque, and their whole concern and aspirations were directed toward it, without regard to the occurrence of the acts by the will of Allah, for they had no doubt or suspicion about that.

This meaning is emphasized by placing the apodosis before the condition, which is either the apodosis itself, according to the more correct of the two opinions as established earlier, or indicates the apodosis, which is omitted and whose placement is delayed, and in either view the fronting of the apodosis or of what indicates it reflects concern for the matter and focuses intention upon it.

It is also emphasized by its confirmation with the lam indicating an implied oath, as if it were said: "By Allah, you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque."

All of this shows you that this is the intended meaning.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 48, verse 28:

Then He informed them that it is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, so that He may make it prevail over all religion. Allah has guaranteed the completion and the triumph of this matter over all the religions of the people of the earth. In this there is a strengthening of their hearts, good news for them, and steadfastness, and that they should be confident of this promise, which He will surely fulfil. So do not think that what occurred of concession and subjugation at al-Hudaybiyyah was a victory for His enemy, or an abandonment of His Messenger and his religion. How could that be, when He sent him with the religion of truth and promised him that He would make it prevail over every other religion?

(Fa'ida)

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religion. And sufficient is Allah as Witness.﴾

He makes it prevail in two ways: a prevailing by proof, clarification and demonstration, and a prevailing by victory, triumph, dominance and support, until He makes it prevail over those who oppose it, and it is made victorious.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned His Messenger and the party (ḥizb) whom He chose for him, and praised them in the best of praise, and mentioned their attributes in the Torah and the Gospel. In this there is among the greatest proofs of the truthfulness of the one who brought the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an, and that these are the ones mentioned in the earlier scriptures with these well-known attributes, not as the disbelievers say about them: that they are domineering seekers of kingship and worldly gain. For this reason, when the Christians of Syria saw them and witnessed their guidance, their conduct, their justice, their knowledge, their mercy, their asceticism in this world and their desire for the Hereafter, they said: "Those who accompanied the Messiah were not better than these." These Christians knew the Companions and their virtue better than the Rafidah, their enemies, and the Rafidah describe them with the opposite of what Allah described them with in this verse and others, and: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one rightly guided; and whomever He leads astray, you will not find for him any guiding ally﴾ [al-Kahf: 17].

(A subtle point)
Consider how from his description two names were derived for the Prophet ﷺ that correspond to its meaning: Aḥmad and Muḥammad. He is Muḥammad because of the abundance of praiseworthy attributes in him, and Aḥmad because of the nobility and excellence of these attributes over the attributes of others. The name is thus bound to the one named as the spirit is bound to the body.

(A benefit)
The words of the Most High: ﴿And their likeness in the Gospel is like a seed that sends out its shoot, then strengthens it, so it grows thick and stands firm on its stalk, pleasing the sowers, that He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾.
Enraging the disbelievers is a goal beloved to the Lord and sought by Him, so agreeing with Him in it is from the perfection of servitude.

(Chapter: on the meaning of the Prophet's name [Muhammad] ﷺ and its derivation)
This name is the most famous of his names ﷺ. It is a name transferred from ḥamd (praise). Originally it is a passive participle (ism mafʿūl) from ḥamd, which includes lauding the one praised, loving him, revering him and magnifying him; this is the true reality of ḥamd. It is formed on the pattern mafʿal, like muʿaẓẓam, muḥabbab, musawwad, mubajjal and their counterparts, because this pattern is established for intensification. If an active participle is derived from it, its meaning is one from whom the act proceeds repeatedly, time after time, like muʿallim, mufhim, mubayyin, mukhlis, mufarrij and the like. If a passive participle is derived from it, its meaning is one upon whom the act occurs repeatedly, time after time, either by entitlement or in fact. So Muḥammad is one whose praise by the praisers is abundant, time after time, or one who deserves to be praised time after time.
It is said: ḥamida, so he is muḥammad, just as it is said: ʿalima, so he is muʿallam. This is a name and a descriptive attribute, and both meanings are united in regard to him ﷺ, even though it is purely a name in regard to many others who were named with it.
This is the case with the names of the Lord, the names of His Book and the names of His Prophet: they are proper names indicating meanings by which they are also descriptions. So there is no contradiction between being a proper name and being a descriptor. Thus He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner, the Subduer; these are names indicating meanings which are His attributes. Likewise the Qur'an, the Criterion, the Clear Book and other of His names.
Likewise the names of the Prophet ﷺ: Muḥammad, Aḥmad, al-Māḥī. In the hadith of Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "I have names: I am Muḥammad, I am Aḥmad, and I am al-Māḥī (the Eraser), through whom Allah erases disbelief."
So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned these names, clarifying what Allah had singled him out with of excellence, and pointing to their meanings. Otherwise, if they were purely proper names without meaning, they would not indicate praise. For this reason Ḥassān, may Allah be pleased with him, said:
"He derived for him a name from His own name, to honor him: the Lord of the Throne is Maḥmūd, and this is Muḥammad."
Likewise all the names of the Lord, the Most High, are names of praise. If they were mere words without meanings, they would not indicate praise. Allah, glorified is He, has described them as all beautiful, saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 180].
So they are not "beautiful" merely by the utterance, but by their indication of the attributes of perfection. For this reason, when some Arabs heard a reciter recite: ﴿As for the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, as a punishment from Allah; and Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾ and he recited "and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful," the Arab said: "This is not the speech of Allah." The reciter said: "Do you deny the speech of Allah?" He said: "No, but this is not the speech of Allah." So the reciter went back to his memorization and recited "and Allah is Mighty, Wise." The Arab said: "You are right: He is Mighty, so He ruled, and He cut off. Had He forgiven and shown mercy, He would not have cut off."
For this reason, when a verse of mercy is concluded with a name of punishment, or the reverse, the incongruity of the speech and its lack of coherence becomes apparent. In the Sunan, from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, the Qur'an was recited in seven ḥurūf (modes), then he said: "None of them is except sufficient and adequate, so long as you do not end a verse of punishment with mercy or a verse of mercy with punishment, [if you say samīʿan ʿalīman, ʿazīzan ḥakīman]." [Its chain is ṣaḥīḥ.]
Had these names been purely proper names without meaning, there would be no difference between concluding a verse with this or with that.
Also, He, glorified is He, gives reasons for His rulings and actions by His names, and if they had no meaning, the reasoning would not be valid, as in His words: ﴿Ask forgiveness of your Lord; indeed He is ever Forgiving﴾ [Nūḥ: 10].
And His words: ﴿For those who swear off their wives there is a waiting period of four months. And if they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. And if they resolve on divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226–227].
So the ruling of return (fayʾ), which is going back and returning to the wife's pleasure and kindness toward her, was concluded with "Forgiving, Merciful," meaning that He returns to His servant with His forgiveness and mercy when he returns to Him. Recompense is of the kind of the deed: just as he returned to what is better, Allah returns to him with forgiveness and mercy. ﴿And if they resolve on divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾.
Since divorce is a spoken word that is heard and an intended meaning, it is followed by the name "Hearing" for its utterance and "Knowing" for its content.
Likewise His words: ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you imply of proposing to women or conceal within yourselves. Allah knows that you will remember them; but do not promise them secretly, except that you say a proper word. And do not determine the marriage contract until the decreed term reaches its end. And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾.
When He, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the allusion to proposing to a woman, which indicates that the one alluding has desire and love for her in his heart, and that this drives him to the speech through which he reaches marriage to her, and lifted the blame from allusion and from the heart's concealment of its inclination and love, and forbade promising them secretly, it was said that this refers to marriage; the meaning being: do not state marriage to them explicitly, except by allusion, which is the proper word. It was also said that it means marrying her secretly during her waiting period, and when the period ends, the contract is made public. This view is supported by His words: ﴿And do not determine the marriage contract until the decreed term reaches its end﴾, which is the end of the waiting period. Whoever prefers the first view says: the verse indicates the permissibility of allusion by lifting blame, the prohibition of explicit statement by negating secret promises, and the prohibition of concluding the marriage contract before the end of the waiting period. If the meaning of secret promise were the secret contract, it would be repetition. Then He followed that with: ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him﴾, meaning: do not transgress what has been set for you, for He is aware of what you conceal and what you disclose. Then He said: ﴿And know that Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾; were it not for His forgiveness and forbearance, you would have fallen into extreme distress. He, glorified is He, observes you, knows what is in your hearts and knows what you do. If you fall into something He has forbidden, then hasten to repentance and seeking forgiveness, for He is the Forgiving, the Forbearing.
This is the method of the Qur'an: it pairs the names of hope with the names of fear, as in His words: ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, and the people of Paradise said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ [Saba': 34].
When they arrived at His honor, by His forgiveness of their sins and His appreciation of their good deeds, they said: "Indeed our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative."
In this is the meaning of causation: that is, by His forgiveness and appreciation we reached the abode of His honor, for He forgave our bad deeds and appreciated our good deeds. And He, Most High, said: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe? And Allah is ever Appreciative and Knowing﴾ [al-Nisā': 147].
This is a reward for their gratitude: that is, if you thank your Lord, He will appreciate your thanks, and He is Knowing of your thanks, nothing of the thanks of one who disbelieves being hidden from Him.
The Qur'an is full of this, and the purpose is to draw attention to it. Also, He, glorified is He, argues by His names for His unity and the negation of partners from Him. If they were names without meaning, they would not indicate this, as in Hārūn's words to the worshippers of the calf: ﴿O my people, you have only been tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 90].
And His words, glorified is He, in the same story: ﴿Indeed your god is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, who has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 98].
And His words, Most High: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163].
And His words, glorified is He, at the end of Surat al-Ḥashr: ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; He is the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the King, the Pure, the Source of Peace, the Giver of Security, the Guardian, the Mighty, the Compelling, the Superior. Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 22–23].
So He glorified and exonerated Himself from the partnership of the polytheists, immediately after praising Himself with His Most Beautiful Names, which necessitate His unity and the impossibility of affirming a partner for Him. Whoever reflects on this meaning in the Qur'an will descend through it into gardens of knowledge that Allah has protected from every liar who turns away from the Book of Allah and from drawing guidance from it. Had this book of ours contained only this section, it would have sufficed anyone who has taste and knowledge. And Allah is the Granter of success to what is right.

Also, Allah Most High attaches to His names complements such as adverbial phrases, prepositional and genitive phrases and others. If they were purely proper names, this would not be valid, as in: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, ﴿For indeed Allah is Knowing of the corrupters﴾, and ﴿And He was ever Merciful to the believers﴾, ﴿Indeed He is Kind and Merciful to them﴾, ﴿And Allah is Competent over all things﴾, ﴿And Allah is Encompassing of the disbelievers﴾, ﴿And Allah was ever Knowing of them﴾, ﴿And Allah was ever Capable over all things﴾ [al-Kahf: 45] (﴿Indeed He is Seeing of what they do﴾), ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, ﴿Indeed He is Aware of His servants, Seeing﴾.
And their counterparts are numerous.

Also, He, glorified is He, makes His names evidence for the attributes of perfection that the deniers reject, as in His words: ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted﴾ [al-Mulk: 14].

The theologians have differed about these names: are they distinct, in view of the distinctness of their meanings, so that each name indicates something other than what the other indicates; or are they synonymous, since they indicate one essence, so their referent is not multiple, and this is the nature of synonyms? The dispute over this is verbal.

The verified view is to say: they are synonymous with respect to the essence, and distinct with respect to the attributes. Each of them indicates the essence described by that attribute by correspondence (muṭābaqa), indicates one of the two alone by inclusion (taḍammun), and indicates the other attribute by implication (iltizām).

(Chapter)
Given this is established, His naming the Prophet ﷺ with this name is because of what it includes of its referent, which is praise. He ﷺ is praised with Allah, praised with His angels, praised with his brothers among the messengers, and praised with all the people of the earth, even if some of them disbelieve in him, for the attributes of perfection in him are praiseworthy to every intelligent person, even if he denies his intellect out of obstinacy, or ignorance of his being characterized by them. Had he known that he was characterized by them, he would have praised him, for one praises the one who has the attributes of perfection even while being ignorant of their presence in him; so he is in reality a praiser of him. He ﷺ was singled out from the referent of praise with what has not been gathered for anyone else. His name is Muḥammad and Aḥmad, and his community, the praisers (al-ḥammādūn), praise Allah in times of ease and hardship. The beginning of their prayer is with praise, the beginning of their sermon is with praise, and their book begins with praise, thus with Allah in the Preserved Tablet. His caliphs and companions will write the Muṣḥaf beginning with praise. In his hand is the banner of praise on the Day of Resurrection. When he prostrates before his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, for intercession, and is permitted to intercede, he praises his Lord with praises that Allah will open to him at that time. He is the owner of the Praiseworthy Station (al-maqām al-maḥmūd), which the first and the last will envy him for.
Allah, Most High, said: ﴿And from the night, pray with it as an additional prayer for you; perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ [al-Isrā': 79], according to the meaning of the Praiseworthy Station. Let one consult what the early generations of the Companions and the Followers said about it in the exegesis of this surah, such as the tafsir of Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Jarīr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, and other tafsirs of the salaf.

Ibn al-Qayyim's Tafsir (Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 48, verse 29 (part 2 of 3):

When he stands at the station (al-maqam), all the people of the gathering praise him then, both the believers and the disbelievers, the first of them and the last of them. He is praised (ﷺ) for what he filled the earth with of guidance, faith, beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds; through him he opened hearts, and through him he dispelled the darkness from the people of the earth, and he rescued them from the captivity of Satan, from polytheism (shirk) with Allah, from disbelief in Him and from ignorance of Him, until through him his followers attained the honour of this world and the Hereafter. For his message reached the people of the earth when they were most in need of it, since they were among worshippers of idols, worshippers of crosses, worshippers of fire, and worshippers of the stars, and those who earn the anger (maghdub alayhim), who have returned with the wrath of Allah, and who are bewildered, not knowing a Lord to worship nor how to worship Him. People devoured one another: whoever found something good would call to it, and fight whoever opposed him. There was no spot of earth illuminated by the light of prophethood. Allah, glorified is He, looked at the people of the earth at that time and despised them, Arab and non-Arab alike, except for remnants upon traces of a sound religion. So Allah relieved the lands and the servants through him, dispelled through him those darknesses, and brought the creation back to life after death. He guided through him from misguidance, taught through him from ignorance, multiplied them after their scarcity, exalted them through him after their humiliation, enriched them through him after their poverty, and opened through him blind eyes, deaf ears and veiled hearts. So people came to know their Lord and their Object of worship to the utmost degree of knowledge their faculties can attain. He repeated, summarised, and elaborated at length on the mention of His names, attributes and actions, until His knowledge became manifest in the hearts of His believing servants, and the clouds of doubt and suspicion were dispelled from them as the clouds part from the moon on the night it is full. He left his community no need in this acquaintance, neither with anyone before him nor with anyone after him; rather, it sufficed them, healed them and made them independent of everyone who has spoken on this subject. ﴿Is it not enough for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them? Surely in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe﴾ [al-Ankabut: 51].

Abu Dawud related in his Marasil from the Prophet ﷺ that he saw in the hand of one of his companions a piece of the Torah, and he said: "Is it not enough for a people of misguidance to follow a book other than their own book that was sent down to their prophet?" Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down, confirming that: ﴿Is it not enough for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them? Surely in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe﴾.

So this is the state of one who takes his religion from a book revealed other than to the Prophet ﷺ; how much more so of one who takes it from the intellect of so-and-so and so-and-so, and prefers that over the words of Allah and His Messenger.

He made known to them the path leading them to their Lord, His pleasure and the abode of His honour, and he did not leave any good thing without commanding them to it, nor any evil thing without forbidding them from it, as he ﷺ said: "I have not left anything that brings you closer to Paradise except that I have commanded you to it, and nothing that brings you closer to the Fire except that I have forbidden you from it."

Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ died while no bird flaps its wings in the sky except that he gave us knowledge of it."

He made known to them their state after meeting their Lord in the most complete manner, so he uncovered the matter and clarified it; he did not leave any door of beneficial knowledge that brings the servants closer to their Lord unopened, nor any difficulty unexplained and unelucidated, until Allah guided hearts through him from their misguidance, healed them through him from their diseases, and relieved them through him from their ignorance. So what human being is more deserving of being praised than him (ﷺ), and may He reward him on behalf of his community with the best of rewards.

The more correct of the two opinions regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 107] is that it is general (in its scope), and on this interpretation there are two aspects.

The first: the generality of "the worlds" means they all gain benefit from his message. As for his followers, they gained through it the honour of this world and the Hereafter. As for his enemies who fought against him, their being killed quickly and dying is better for them than their living, because their life only adds to the intensification of their punishment in the Hereafter, and they have already been decreed wretchedness; so hastening their death is better for them than prolonging their lives in disbelief. As for those with whom he had a covenant, they lived in this world under his shade, his pact and his protection, and they were less harmful through that covenant than those who waged war against him.

As for the hypocrites, through their outward profession of faith in him they obtained the protection of their blood, their wealth and their families, the respect for these, and the application of the rulings of the Muslims to them in matters of inheritance and other things. As for the distant nations, Allah, glorified is He, through his message lifted the general punishment from the people of the earth, so all the worlds gained benefit from his message.

The second aspect: he is a mercy to everyone, but the believers accepted this mercy and benefited from it in this world and the next, while the disbelievers rejected it; yet this does not take him out of being a mercy to them, though they did not accept it. It is like saying: "This is a medicine for this illness." If the patient does not use it, it does not cease to be a medicine for that illness.

Among the things for which he ﷺ is to be praised is the noble character Allah created him with (see the beginning of Surah al-Qalam) and his generous dispositions. Whoever considers his character and dispositions ﷺ knows that they are the best character of creation and the most noble traits of creation. He ﷺ was the most knowledgeable of creation, the greatest of them in trustworthiness, the most truthful in speech, the most forbearing, the most generous, the most liberal, the most patient in enduring hardship, the greatest in pardon and forgiveness, and the increase of ignorance directed at him would only increase him in forbearance.

As al-Bukhari related in his Sahih from Abdullah ibn Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said about the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the Torah: "Muhammad, My servant and My messenger. I have named him al-Mutawakkil (the one who relies upon Allah). He is not harsh, nor coarse, nor clamorous in the markets, and he does not repay evil with evil, but he pardons and overlooks. I will not take him until he establishes the crooked nation by their saying: there is no god but Allah, and opens with him blind eyes, deaf ears and veiled hearts."

He was the most merciful and compassionate of creation towards them, and the greatest of creation in benefit to them in their religion and their worldly life; the most eloquent of God's creation and the best at expressing many meanings in concise words that indicate the intended meaning; the most patient in the situations requiring patience; the most truthful in the situations of encounter; the most faithful to covenant and protection; the greatest in repaying a kindness with much more than its like; the most humble; the greatest in preferring others over himself; the strongest of creation in defending his companions, protecting them and shielding them; the most upright of creation in what he commands and the most distant from what he forbids; and the one most joined to his kin. So he is most deserving of the words of the poet:

"Gentle to the near and merciful, and to the enemies, a hard, firm hide."

Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the most generous of people in heart, the most truthful in speech, the gentlest in disposition, and the most honourable in companionship. Whoever saw him at first sight was awed by him, and whoever mixed with him in acquaintance loved him. His describer would say: I have not seen anyone like him before or after him (ﷺ)."

So his saying "he was the most generous of people in heart" means generosity of heart, abundance of his goodness, that goodness gushed forth from him in torrents, and that he embodied every beautiful character and every good, as some scholars said: "There is no place in the whole world that contained more goodness than the heart of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; he gathered goodness in its entirety and deposited it in his heart (ﷺ)."

His saying "the most truthful in speech" is something his enemies who waged war against him acknowledged; none of his enemies ever found him guilty of a single lie, to say nothing of the testimony of all his allies to that. The people of the earth fought him with all kinds of warfare, both polytheists and People of the Book, and none of them ever once accused him of a single lie, small or great.

Al-Miswar ibn Makhramah said: "I said to Abu Jahl, and he was my maternal uncle: 'O uncle, did you used to accuse Muhammad of lying before he made his statement?' He said: 'By Allah, O nephew of my sister, Muhammad, when he was a young man, was called among us al-Amin (the trustworthy). When grey hair appeared on him, he would not have lied.' I said: 'O uncle, why do you not follow him?' He said: 'O nephew of my sister, we and the Banu Hashim competed for honour: they fed and we fed, they gave drink and we gave drink, they granted protection and we granted protection. When we knelt side by side and were like two horses in a race, they said: "From us is a prophet." So when will we attain this?' Or as he said."

The Exalted said, consoling him and making light for him the words of his enemies: ﴿We know indeed that what they say grieves you; but it is not you they deny, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah. Messengers were denied before you, and they were patient over what they were denied and harmed, until Our help reached them. There is none who can change the words of Allah. And indeed some of the news of the messengers has come to you﴾ [al-An'am: 33-34].

His saying "the gentlest in disposition" means: easy, soft, close to the people, responsive to the call of whoever calls him, fulfilling the need of whoever asks him to, a consoler of the heart of whoever approaches him, not depriving him nor turning him away disappointed. If his companions wanted something from him, he would agree with them and follow them in it; and if he resolved upon a matter, he would not act on his own apart from them, but would consult them and seek their counsel. He would accept from the good among them and pardon the wrongdoer among them.

His saying "the most honourable in companionship" means that he never kept company with a companion except in the most complete and finest and most honourable companionship. He would not frown in his face, nor be harsh with him in speech, nor withhold his cheerfulness from him, nor hold against him the slips of his tongue, nor take him to account for what proceeded from him of rudeness and the like; rather, he would treat his companion with the utmost kindness and bear with him to the utmost degree of forbearance. So his companionship with them consisted of bearing their harm and their rudeness entirely; he would not punish any of them, nor blame him, nor confront him with what he disliked. Whoever mixed with him would say: "I am the most beloved of people to him," because of what he saw of his gentleness towards him, his nearness to him, his turning towards him, his concern for his affair, his sacrifice for him, the lavishing of kindness upon him and the bearing of his rudeness. What companionship has been, or will be, more honourable than this companionship?

Al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I asked my father about the conduct of the Prophet ﷺ with his companions, and he said: The Prophet ﷺ was constantly cheerful, easy in disposition, gentle in manner; not harsh, nor coarse, nor clamorous, nor foul-tongued, nor faultfinding, nor excessively praising. He overlooked what he did not desire, and did not disappoint whoever hoped in him, nor leave him empty-handed. He had abandoned himself of three things: disputation, excess, and what did not concern him. He did not disparage anyone, nor blame him, nor seek his faults, and he spoke only in what he hoped for its reward. When he spoke, his companions lowered their heads as if birds were upon their heads. When he was silent, they spoke; they did not dispute in his presence over speech, and whoever spoke in his presence they listened to until he finished. Their talk was like their first talk. He laughed at what they laughed at and marvelled at what they marvelled at, and he would bear patiently with the stranger's rudeness in speech and questioning, until his companions would bring such people to him. He said: 'When you see one seeking a need, help him.' He would not accept praise except from one who reciprocates, and he would not cut off anyone's speech until he passed its limit, then he would cut it off with a prohibition or by standing up."

His saying "whoever saw him at first sight was awed by him, and whoever mixed with him in acquaintance loved him" describes him with two qualities that Allah has singled out for people of truthfulness and sincerity: they are reverence (ijlal) and love (mahabbah). Allah had cast upon him awe and love from Himself, so every one who saw him was in awe of him, honouring him and filling his heart with veneration and reverence, even if he was an enemy to him; but when he mixed with him and kept his company, he became more beloved to him than every creature. So he is the one revered, magnified, beloved and honoured. This is the perfection of love: that it be joined with veneration and awe. Love without awe or veneration is deficient, and awe and veneration without love are also deficient, as they are for the treacherous wrongdoer. Perfection is that love, affection, veneration and reverence come together; and this is not found except when the beloved possesses the attributes of perfection that make him deserving of being venerated and loved for them.

Since Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is more deserving of this than anyone, He is the one deserving to be venerated, magnified, held in awe, loved and cherished with every part of the heart, and no partner should be assigned to Him in that. This is the shirk that Allah, glorified is He, will not forgive: to equate another with Him in this love. The Exalted said: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, rivals; they love them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165].

So He informed that whoever loves something other than Allah in the way he loves Allah has taken it as a rival (nid). The people of the Fire said in the Fire to their objects of worship: ﴿By Allah, we were indeed in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 97-98].

Their equating them with Allah was not in that they created the heavens and the earth, nor that they created them, nor that they created their fathers; rather, they equated them with the Lord of the worlds in love for them, as one loves Allah. The reality of worship is love together with humility, and this is the reverence and honour which He described Himself with in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾ [al-Rahman: 78].

The more correct of the two opinions on this is that "al-jalal" (majesty) is veneration, and "al-ikram" (honour) is love, and this is the secret of the servant's saying: "There is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest." For this reason it came in Musnad Ahmad, from the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Be persistent with: O Possessor of Majesty and Honour." [[Sahih hadith]]

That is, hold fast to it and keep repeating it.

In Musnad Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili, from one of the Companions, that he asked to know the Greatest Name of Allah, and he saw in his dream written in the sky with stars: "O Originator of the heavens and the earth, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour."

Every love and veneration for human beings is only permissible as a derivative of the love of Allah and His veneration, like the love of His Messenger and veneration of him, for it is part of the completeness of love for the one who sent him and veneration of him. His community loves him for Allah's love of him, venerates and honours him for Allah's honouring of him; so it is love for Allah, arising from the requirements of Allah's love. Likewise the love of the people of knowledge and faith, and the love and honour of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), are a consequence of Allah's and His Messenger's love for them.

The point is that the Prophet ﷺ was cast by Allah, glorified and exalted is He, with awe and love from Him, and every believer who is sincere has a share of that.

Al-Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "Indeed the believer is granted sweetness and awe," meaning he is loved, feared and honoured by what Allah, glorified is He, has clothed him with of the garment of faith, which requires that. For this reason no human being was more beloved to another, nor more awe-inspiring and majestic in his heart, than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in the hearts of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them).

'Amr ibn al-As said, before his Islam: "There was no person more hateful to me than him; but when I embraced Islam, there was no person more beloved to me than him, nor more magnificent in my eyes. Had I been asked to describe him to you, I could not, because I never filled my eyes with him out of reverence for him."

Urwah ibn Mas'ud said to Quraysh: "O people, by Allah, I have been received by Kisra, Caesar and the kings, and I have never seen a king whose companions venerate him as the companions of Muhammad venerate Muhammad ﷺ. By Allah, they do not lower their gaze towards him out of veneration for him. When he spits, his spittle falls into the palm of one of them, who rubs it over his face and chest; and when he performs ablution, they nearly fight over his ablution water."

Since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ embodied what calls for him to be praised again and again, he was named Muhammad, a name that matches its bearer and a word that corresponds to its meaning.

The difference between the wording of Ahmad and Muhammad is in two respects:

The first of them: Muhammad is the one praised with repeated praise, so the name indicates the great number of those who praise him, and that entails a great number of reasons for praise in him. Ahmad is the elative (af'al al-tafdil) form from praise, indicating that the praise he deserves is superior to what others deserve. So Muhammad denotes an increase in praise in quantity, and Ahmad an increase in quality. Thus he is praised with the most praise and the best praise that mankind has offered.

The second aspect: Muhammad is the one praised with repeated praise, as previously explained, and Ahmad is the one whose praise of his Lord is superior to the praise of other praisers. So one of the two names, Muhammad, indicates that he is praised, and the second name, Ahmad, indicates that he is the most praiseworthy of those who praise their Lord. This is the analogical reasoning, for the elative and the exclamatory forms, according to a group of the Basran grammarians, are formed only from the verb of the doer (fa'il), and are not formed from the verb of the object (maf'ul). Their basis is that the elative and exclamatory forms are formed only from the intransitive verb (lazim), not from the transitive (muta'addi). For this reason they posit that the verb is transferred from the pattern fa'ala or fa'ila to the pattern fa'ula (with a damma on the 'ayn). They said: the evidence for this is that it becomes transitive to the object by the hamza, so the hamza in it is for transitivity, as in ma azraf Zaydan (how elegant is Zayd!) and akram 'Amran (how generous is 'Amr!), and their origins are zarufa and karuma.

They said: because the one being admired is originally the doer, so its verb must be non-transitive.

They said: as for their saying ma adraba Zaydan li-'Amr (how much does Zayd strike 'Amr!), its verb is transitive originally.

They said: it is transferred from darraba to the pattern of the intransitive verb, then it was made transitive from the verb by the hamza of transitivity.

They said: the evidence for this is their bringing the lam, so they say ma adraba Zaydan li-'Amr. Had it remained transitive as it was, one would say ma adraba Zaydan 'Amran, because it is transitive to one directly and to the other by the hamza of transitivity. So when it was made transitive to the object by the hamza of transitivity, it was made transitive to the other by the lam, and thus it is known to be intransitive. This is what made them say that this is formed only from the verb of the doer, not from the verb falling upon the object.

Others disputed this and said: it is permissible to form the verb of exclamation and elation from the verb of the doer and from the verb falling upon the object. The Arabs say: ma ashghalahu bi-al-shay' (how absorbed he is in the thing!), and this is from shughila bihi, on the pattern of su'ila. So the admiration is of the one occupied with the thing, not of the occupier. Likewise their saying ma awla'ahu bi-kadha (how fond he is of such-and-such!) is from uwliya bihi, built in the passive. For the Arabs have committed this verb to the passive form and did not build it in the active. Likewise their saying ma a'jabahu bi-kadha (how amazed he is by such-and-such!) is from u'jiba bi-al-shay'. Likewise their saying ma ahabbahu ilayya (how dear he is to me!) is an exclamation from the verb of the object. Likewise their saying ma abghadahu ilayya and ma amqatahu ilayya.

Here is a well-known issue mentioned by Sibawayh, namely that you say ma abghadani lahu and ma ahabbani lahu and ma amqatani lahu when you are the one who hates, the one who loathes, and so it is an exclamation about the act of the doer. And you say ma abghadani ilayhi and ma amqatani ilayhi and ma ahabbani ilayhi when you are the one hated, the one loathed, or the one loved, and so it is an exclamation about the act falling upon the object. So what is with lam is for the doer, and what is with ila is for the object. Likewise you say ma ahabbahu ilayya when he is the one loved, and ma abghadahu ilayya when he is the one who hates. Most grammarians do not give a reason for this.

What is said about its cause, and God knows best, is that the lam in meaning belongs to the doer, as in your saying to whom this act belongs, so you say li-Zayd and bring the lam. As for ila, it is for the object in meaning, because one says to whom this act arrives, so you say ila Zayd.

The secret of this is that the lam originally denotes ownership or specification, and entitlement. Ownership and entitlement belong only to the doer who owns and deserves. Ila denotes the end of a limit, and the limit is the furthest point of what the act requires, so it is more fitting for the object, because it completes what the act requires. From the exclamation about the act of the object is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr about the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Then he is more fearsome to me when I speak to him, and it is said you are imprisoned and slain,
from a lion of the lions, the lions of the wild, whose lair is in the belly of 'Athar, a thicket within a thicket."

So akhwaf here is from khuffa, not from khafa, and it is the counterpart of Ahmad from Muhammad, as su'ila is the counterpart of hamida, as 'ulima. And you say ma ajannahu from junna, so he is majnun.

The Basrans said: all this is anomalous and not to be relied upon.

Others said: this has become very common in their speech, and treating it as anomaly is not permissible, because the anomalous is what contradicts their usage and the regular pattern of their speech, and this does not contradict that.

They said: as for your assumption that the verb is intransitive and its transfer to the pattern of the damma-'ayn verb, no evidence supports it.

As for what you rely on regarding transitivity by the hamza, it is not as you have stated. The hamza here is not for transitivity; it is for indicating the meaning of exclamation and elation, like the alif of the doer, the mim of the object, and the ta' of the reflexive and passive form, and similar letters that attach to the triliteral verb to show the addition it receives beyond its bare meaning. This is the reason that brings this alif, not merely the transitivity of the verb.

They said: what shows this is that the verb made transitive by the hamza may also be made transitive by a preposition or by doubling. You say ajlastu Zaydan and jalastuhu and jalasta bihi, aqamtuhu and qawwamtuhu and qumta bihi, and anamtuhu and nawwamtuhu and nimta bihi, and similar. Here nothing other than the hamza can take its place, so it is invalid that it is for transitivity.

Second, it combines with the ba' of transitivity, so you say akram bihi and ahsan bihi, meaning ma akramahu and ma ahsanahu, and a verb cannot be made transitive by two transitivity markers together.

Third, they say ma a'taha Zaydan lid-darahim (how much he gave Zayd the dirhams!) and ma akssahu lith-thiyab (how much he clothed him in garments!). This is from a'ta and kasa, the transitive verbs, and it is not valid to posit its transfer from 'ata when it means to take, and then to add the hamza of transitivity, as some interpreted it, because the meaning is corrupted. The exclamation falls on his giving, not on his taking, and the hamza in it is the hamza of exclamation and elation, and the hamza of its own verb has been dropped, so it cannot be said that it is for transitivity.

They said: as for your saying that it is made transitive by the lam in their saying ma adraba Zaydan li-'Amr, and were it not intransitive it would not be made transitive by the lam, this is not as you have stated regarding the intransitivity of the verb. Rather it is strengthening for it, because it was weakened by being barred from declension and made to follow one fixed pattern, so it left the normal course of verbs and became weak in its requirement, so it was strengthened by the lam. This is like how it is strengthened by the lam when its complement precedes it and it receives a kind of weakness from being placed before, and they compensate with the lam, as God says: ﴿If you are interpreters of dreams, interpret it﴾ [Yusuf: 43]. And as it is strengthened by the lam when it is an active participle, as you say: ana muhibbun laka (I am loving to you) and mukrimun li-Zayd and the like. So when this verb was weakened by being barred from declension, it was strengthened by the lam.

This view is the preponderant one, as you see. And God knows best.

Returning to the intended point: he (ﷺ) was named Muhammad and Ahmad because he is praised more than others praise anyone and better than others are praised. Thus both names are in the passive sense, the object of praise. This is the preferred view, and it is more eloquent in his praise and more complete in meaning. Had the intended meaning been that of the doer, he would have been named Hammad, meaning one who praises much, just as he was named Muhammad, meaning one praised much. For he (ﷺ) was the most praising of creation to his Lord. So if his name were by consideration of the doer, it would have been more fitting to name him Hammad, just as the name of his community is al-Hammadun (those who praise much).

Moreover, both names are derived from his praiseworthy character and qualities, for which he deserved to be named Muhammad and Ahmad. He is the one praised by the people of this world and the Hereafter, and praised by the people of heaven and earth. Because of the abundance of his praiseworthy qualities, which exceed the count of those who count, he was named with two of the names of praise, which imply superiority and increase in quantity and attribute. And God knows best.
